articles.body: Star Bulk Carriers Corp. Reports Net Profit Of $141.9 Million For The Third Quarter Of 2026 in Hellenic Shipping News 19/11/2026 Star Bulk Carriers Corp., a global shipping company focusing on the transportation of dry bulk cargoes, today announced its unaudited financial and operating results for the third quarter of 2026. Unless otherwise indicated or unless the context requires otherwise, all references in this press release to “we,” “us,” “our,” or similar references, mean Star Bulk Carriers Corp. and, where applicable, its consolidated subsidiaries. Petros Pappas, Chief Executive Officer of Star Bulk, commented: “Star Bulk delivered another strong quarter, with Net Income of $141.9 million, EBITDA of $192.6 million, and a TCE of $24,616 per vessel per day for the third quarter of 2026. In line with our full payout policy, the Board has declared a dividend of $1.00 per share, up from $0.90 last quarter and our 23rd consecutive quarterly dividend. Since 2021, we will have returned over $2.27 billion to shareholders, comprising $1.68 billion in dividends and $0.59 billion in share repurchases, representing approximately 70% of our current market capitalization. In September, we completed the parallel listing of our shares on Euronext Athens, alongside an equity offering that raised gross proceeds of €107.8 million ($124.4 million). The listing gives us access to the European capital markets, broadens our shareholder base to include European and euro-based investors, and extends trading in our shares across European and U.S. market hours. On the fleet, we have completed our newbuilding program, with the last of our 8 latest-generation Kamsarmaxes delivered in November. We have also entered into a strategic partnership with Hermes World Maritime on two of these vessels, expanding our relationship with an established shipping group, and we will continue to explore opportunities to grow our partnership further. Our balance sheet remains the among the strongest in the sector. Our cash as of November 18, 2026, stood at $766 million against total debt of $1,041 million, resulting in net debt of only $275 million. This corresponds to attractively low net leverage against our total assets of 6% and of 26% against the demolition value of our fleet. With this level of financial strength, we have the capacity to act decisively and scale up when attractive opportunities arise to create long-term value for our shareholders. Heading into year-end, we are constructive on the dry bulk market, supported by tonne-mile growth, port congestion and trade route disruptions, as well as favorable seasonality. Star Bulk remains one of the best platforms for investors to participate in the dry bulk market, with a large, diversified and efficient fleet, an industry-leading cost structure, and a simple, shareholder-friendly capital allocation policy.” Recent Developments Declaration of Dividend On November 18, 2026, our Board of Directors declared a quarterly cash dividend of $1.00 per share, payable on December 11, 2026 to all shareholders of record as of December 1, 2026, which will be the record date for both the Nasdaq and Euronext Athens markets. The ex-dividend date established by Nasdaq is expected to be December 1, 2026. The ex-dividend date for dividends payable to holders of shares via Euronext Securities Athens is expected to be November 30, 2026. Parallel Listing and Offering in Greece On September 15, 2026, we announced the settlement of the offering of a total of 4,400,000 common shares at a price of €24.50 ($28.27)1 per share, resulting in gross proceeds of €107.8 million ($124.4 million)1, and the admission to parallel listing of all our common shares on the Main Market of the Regulated Securities Market of Euronext Athens (“Euronext Athens”). Trading of our common shares on Euronext Athens commenced on September 16, 2026. As of the date of this release, we have 116,071,386 common shares outstanding. Fleet Update Vessels’ S&P The previously announced sales of the vessels Pendulum and Star Eva were completed on July 6, 2026 and September 8, 2026, respectively. In connection with the two sales, we collected proceeds of approximately $31.9 million, net of commissions. Newbuilding Vessel Program Update In August 2026, we took delivery of two newbuilding vessels, the Star Bella and the Star Kyra. During the third quarter of 2026, we made payments of $56.5 million in connection with our Newbuilding Vessel Program. The three remaining newbuilding vessels Star Argyro, Star Irini and Star Aline, were delivered to us in October and November 2026 and we paid $65.0 million in delivery instalments during that period. Financing On September 30, 2026, we entered into an agreement for a Japanese Operating Lease with Call Options (“JOLCO”), providing financing of $35.2 million related to the recently delivered newbuilding vessel Star Kyra. The financing was drawn on October 20, 2026. On October 9, 2026, we entered into a strategic partnership with Hermes World Maritime S.A. (“Hermes”), involving the two recently delivered newbuilding Kamsarmax vessels, Star Ellie and Star Bella. Under this partnership, Hermes acquired a 35% ownership interest in the companies owning the two vessels for total proceeds of approximately $24.6 million. Star Bulk will continue to perform the vessels’ commercial and technical management. On November 17, 2026, we drew down the remaining $78.0 million available under our E-SUN $130.0 million Facility. The amount of $78.0 million drawn under the ESUN $130.0 million Facility is repayable within seven years from the applicable drawdown date. As of the date of this press release we have 28 unlevered vessels. Third Quarter 2026 and 2025 Results For the third quarter of 2026, we had net income of $141.9 million, or $1.26 earnings per share, compared to net income for the third quarter of 2025 of $18.5 million, or $0.16 earnings per share. Adjusted Net income, which excludes certain non-cash items, was $143.8 million, or $1.28 adjusted earnings per share, for the third quarter of 2026, compared to an Adjusted Net income of $32.4 million, or $0.28 adjusted earnings per share for the third quarter of 2025. Net cash provided by operating activities for the third quarter of 2026 was $161.0 million, compared to $91.8 million for the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA, which excludes certain non-cash items, was $194.5 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $86.8 million for the third quarter of 2025. Voyage revenues for the third quarter of 2026 increased to $366.9 million from $263.9 million in the corresponding period of 2025, and Time charter equivalent revenues (“TCE Revenues”)2 increased to $293.7 million from $202.3 million. Despite the decrease in the average number of vessels in our fleet to 134.8 from 141.4, the increase in Voyage revenues and TCE Revenues were primarily attributable to the higher charter rates prevailing in the recent period, as also reflected in the increase in the TCE rate2 to $24,616 for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $16,634 for the third quarter of 2025. Charter-in hire expenses for the third quarter of 2026 decreased to $12.8 million, compared with $15.4 million in the third quarter of 2025. This decrease was primarily attributable to a decrease in charter-in days to 768 in the third quarter of 2026 from 899 in the corresponding period in 2025. Vessel operating expenses for the third quarter of 2026 decreased to $65.3 million, compared to $67.8 million for the third quarter of 2025, primarily due to the decrease in the average number of vessels in our fleet. Daily operating expenses per vessel, excluding pre-delivery expenses due to change of management and delivery of our newbuilding vessels, remained relatively stable at $5,171 for the third quarter of 2026 compared to $5,096 for the corresponding period of 2025. Dry docking expenses for the third quarter of 2026 amounted to $17.1 million, compared to $28.1 million for the corresponding period in 2025. During the third quarter of 2026, nine vessels completed their scheduled periodic dry docking surveys, including three vessels whose dry dockings commenced in the preceding quarter, compared to 14 vessels in the third quarter of 2025, including two vessels whose dry dockings commenced in the preceding quarter. The decrease in dry docking expenses was primarily attributable to the lower number of vessels undergoing and completing scheduled dry dockings during the third quarter of 2026, as well as the timing of related expenses across reporting periods. General and administrative expenses for the third quarters of 2026 and 2025 were $18.0 million and $19.7 million, respectively, which included share-based compensation of $6.9 million and $7.3 million, respectively. The decrease in general and administrative expenses was primarily attributable to the lower average EUR/USD exchange rate during the third quarter of 2026 ($1.1505 compared to $1.1681 in the corresponding period of 2025), as well as a decrease in the average number of employees, partly driven by the lower average number of vessels in our fleet. Vessel management fees in the third quarter of 2026 amounted to $5.6 million compared to $5.9 million for the corresponding period in 2025. Our daily net cash general and administrative expenses per vessel (including management fees and excluding share-based compensation and other non-cash charges) decreased to $1,260 for the third quarter of 2026 from $1,325 for the third quarter of 2025. Depreciation expense decreased to $40.6 million for the third quarter of 2026 compared to $41.8 million for the corresponding period in 2025. The decrease is driven by the decrease in the average number of vessels in our fleet, as discussed above. During the third quarter of 2026, we recognized a net gain on forward freight agreements (“FFAs”) and bunker swaps of $0.1 million, consisting of an unrealized gain of $0.9 million and a realized loss of $0.9 million. During the third quarter of 2025, we recognized a net loss on FFAs and bunker swaps of $0.1 million, consisting of an unrealized loss of $0.7 million and a realized gain of $0.6 million. During the third quarter of 2026, we recognized a gain on sale of vessels of $4.1 million in connection with the delivery of two sold vessels to their new owners. During the third quarter of 2025, we recognized a loss on sale of vessels of $5.3 million in connection with the completion of sales of three vessels. Interest and finance costs for the third quarters of 2026 and 2025 were $12.5 million and $17.7 million, respectively. The decrease was primarily driven by lower loan interest expense, reflecting a decline in weighted average outstanding indebtedness to $957.2 million in the third quarter of 2026 from $1,126.1 million in the third quarter of 2025, and a decrease in the weighted average interest rate to 5.21% from 5.96% over the same periods. articles.body: Sanctioned Tankers Carry 60% of Russian Oil in October: Monthly Intelligence Report in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 This analysis was produced by Windward’s Maritime Intelligence Operations Center (MIOC), a mission-critical capability powered by Windward’s maritime intelligence experts and operating as a seamless extension of your team. This is a sample of what we deliver. Vessel identifiers and ownership entities have been redacted for external distribution; AIS-based assessments are probabilistic and intended solely as decision support, and nothing herein should be construed as evidence of wrongdoing by any vessel, company, or individual. For intelligence tailored to your operational theater, visit the MIOC page. Sanctioned Tankers Carry 60% of Russian Oil in October Sixty percent of Russian oil was shipped on sanctioned tankers throughout October, supported by a rising number of new shadow fleet entrants over 2026 that are being used to offset freight logistics inefficiencies and restrictions. Analysis of tankers calling at Russian ports to load crude, fuel oil and refined products last month found that EU-owned tankers shipped 14% of volumes, one of the lowest percentages recorded this year. Unsanctioned shadow fleet tankers accounted for 21% of all oil shipments, according to Windward analysis using data from Vortexa. Sanctioned tankers were mostly used for crude shipments (69% of barrels shipped), followed by refined products (42%) and fuel oil (30%). The overall figure of 60% carried on sanctioned tankers compares with 55% in September and 67% in March. Russia Secures New Unsanctioned Tonnage The October numbers underscore the rapidly changing composition of the sanctions-circumventing shadow fleet, and Russia’s ability to secure new, unsanctioned tonnage to support its freight logistics. Tankers that are sanctioned are reflagging to Russia and changing registered ownership to SVPs in China, Hong Kong, and Russia. Meanwhile, new companies are being formed to buy and deploy fresh and existing shadow fleet tonnage that has yet to be targeted by regulators. Naval Boardings Push Sanctioned Tankers To Reflag to Russian Of the 143 sanctioned tankers tracked calling at Russian Baltic, Black Sea, Arctic and Far East ports in October, 48% (69 ships) were flagged with Russia. Of those 69 ships, 31 have switched to the Russian flag in the past six months. The reflagging was triggered by a new strategy implemented by EU and UK naval forces over 2026 to board and interdict stateless or falsely flagged tankers. The remainder of sanctioned tonnage is flagged with Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Sierra Leone, or Oman. These ship registries continue to provide services to UK- or EU-sanctioned tankers, but not U.S.-sanctioned. No falsely flagged tonnage was noted loading Russian oil this month, the fourth consecutive month. There are several Russia-linked falsely flagged tankers observed loitering in the Mediterranean but do not appear to be active in shipping oil. Unsanctioned Tankers Step In to Supplement the Shadow Fleet The EU and UK have together blacklisted nearly 700 shadow fleet tankers over the past two-and-a-half years, disrupting the supply chain. Sanctions make it harder — but not impossible — for these ships to continue trading without links to Western marine service providers. The rise in unsanctioned shadow fleet tankers to replace and/or supplement the work of the inefficient sanctioned fleet is of particular interest, especially since EU regulations are in place that are designed to prevent sales of second-hand vessels for Russia trading. How Windward Defines the Unsanctioned Shadow Fleet Unsanctioned shadow fleet tankers are defined as those aged 15 years or over, solely deployed in Russian trades (including those undertaking two consecutive Russian oil loadings since a change in ownership was noted), with registered ownership and management hidden behind companies in jurisdictions where the beneficial owner cannot be traced. There were 41 unsanctioned shadow fleet tankers tracked shipping Russian oil in October. Of these, nine did not have P&I insurance with marine insurers that were part of the International Group. Of the remaining that did have International Group insurance, 88% were insured with two P&I clubs. There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by marine insurers. The G7 Oil Price Cap allows marine service providers to ship Russian oil to third countries if the price at which oil is sold is below a cap. New Shadow Fleet Clusters Emerge in 2026 The shadow fleet has evolved over the past four years, with tankers having multiple changes of registered owners, flags, and ISM managers across countries and jurisdictions to obfuscate beneficial ownership and evade sanctions. New clusters observed this year include what Windward has called the “Kowloon Cluster,” a group of 45-plus tankers linked by a Hong Kong-based nominee director and Azerbaijan ISM managers. All but three tankers are sanctioned. A UAE-Based Manager Amasses 20 Unsanctioned Tankers The newest cluster observed is a UAE-based cluster of 20 tankers, all unsanctioned. The fleet of 20 Russia-trading tankers began amassing in February via the ISM management of a newly formed United Arab Emirates-based entity. The company gives its address at serviced offices that overlook a racecourse in Dubai. The twenty ships moved to the company’s management between February and October this year. Six of them were unsanctioned but long-established shadow fleet players and connected to two sanctioned clusters. These shipping companies were disbanded in 2023 and linked to Rosneft and Lukoil. Eleven ships were sold directly to the company by EU-owned companies this year. Some but not all had already been deployed in shipping Russian oil under the G7 Oil Price Cap and continued to do so. Ajman-Based Shipmanager Takes Over Five Russia-Trading Tankers An Ajman-based shipmanager manages five shadow fleet tankers, all with registered ownership in China. All five tankers are unsanctioned and have been deployed in Russia trading for well over 18 months. They all entered management between February and May. Russia Imports Fuel as Refinery Attacks Cut Capacity Russian diesel and jet fuel exports over October were tracked by Vortexa at about 350,000 bpd, more than double September’s volumes, at 160,000 bpd. Before Ukraine attacks on Russian refineries accelerated in mid-2026, middle distillate export volumes were at about 800,000 bpd. Russia reportedly extended export bans on gasoline to diesel in July to address domestic shortfalls after attacks on refineries over 2026 left 51% of capacity offline, according to Ukraine’s Defense Ministry as of October 4. Domestic shortages saw Russia importing diesel and gasoline from July, with 115,000 bpd tracked arriving in August, just under 100,000 bpd in September and 70,000 bpd in October. Gasoil exported from a storage terminal at Morocco shipped most of the ~750,000 barrels of gasoil and diesel that were discharged at Russian Baltic ports last month. The U.S. Diesel Waiver Has Yet to Deliver a Cargo In response to a looming global diesel shortage, the U.S. government announced a US import sanctions waiver on Russian diesel on October 9. Despite the waiver, no Russian diesel cargoes have been tracked arriving in the U.S. amid political, compliance and enforcement challenges, especially if tankers are sanctioned by the UK or EU. One likely candidate, a Malta-flagged tanker, reversed course on November 10 about 450 nautical miles from Philadelphia, the probable destination, and had yet to signal a new destination seven days later. Diesel prices remain well above the $100/bbl G7 Oil Price Cap, with global assessments from price reporting agencies in the 190-200/bbl range over the month of October. There were 11 diesel cargoes loaded on tankers with EU ownership identified by Windward using Vortexa data extracted in early November. In order to remain price cap-compliant, Russian oil traders would have sold the cargo at half the price they could have secured in the global market. High Urals Price Tests Price Cap Enforcement According to the Russian Ministry of Economic Development, the average sales price of Urals crude over October was $101.46/barrel. This is 130% above the EU price cap of $44.10 per barrel. The ministry reached its assessment by averaging the price reported by the global price reporting agency, Argus. Argus assessments are used by oil traders worldwide. Like diesel, the high Urals price provides compliance and enforcement challenges for marine service providers with EU, UK, or U.S. exposure. Compliance rests on attestation documents that are provided by the buyer and seller of the oil and cannot be verified by all parties in the marine service chain. Some 7% (8.2 million barrels) of Urals shipped in October were on 12 EU-owned tankers, according to analysis. Source: Windward 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: US ethanol offers lower GHG abatement costs than methanol, ammonia: study
articles.summary: US corn-based ethanol could offer shipowners a cheaper route to reducing greenhouse gas emissions than low-carbon methanol and ammonia, potentially opening a new marine fuel market for American producers as the global fleet of methanol-capable vessels expands, according to a study released last week. articles.body: US ethanol offers lower GHG abatement costs than methanol, ammonia: study in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 US corn-based ethanol could offer shipowners a cheaper route to reducing greenhouse gas emissions than low-carbon methanol and ammonia, potentially opening a new marine fuel market for American producers as the global fleet of methanol-capable vessels expands, according to a study released last week. Ethanol could abate about 2.09 metric tons of CO2 equivalent for every $1,000 spent on fuel, compared with 1.30 mt for low-carbon methanol and 1.73 mt for low-carbon ammonia, the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance, an initiative by the nonprofit Global Centre for Green Fuels, said in the study. MEMA estimated ethanol’s well-to-wake greenhouse gas intensity at 34.9 grams of CO2e/megajoule, compared with 15 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon methanol and 10 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon ammonia. Emissions abatement was calculated against a heavy fuel oil baseline of 93.3 gCO2e/MJ. “Ethanol is a commercially viable fuel when compared to other fuels … [it] delivers maximum carbon abatement per dollar of fuel expenditure among commercially available, scalable marine fuels,” according to the study. In the study, based on classification society ABS’s technical analysis, MEMA assumed US corn ethanol prices on a free-on-board Houston basis at $750/mt, equivalent to $1,125/mt of very low sulfur fuel oil on an energy-adjusted basis. That compared with $1,200/mt, or $2,424/mt on a VLSFO-equivalent basis, for low-carbon methanol and $900/mt, or $1,945/mt VLSFOe, for low-carbon ammonia. VLSFO was assumed at $590/mt. The study’s indicative mid-2026 prices showed ethanol remained substantially more expensive than conventional bunkers but offered lower costs than other low-carbon alternatives. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed FOB Houston ethanol barge prices at 202.25 cents/gallon on Nov. 11, roughly equivalent to $677/mt. Delivered low-carbon methanol bunker prices in the Houston Ship Channel were $1,146.57/mt on the same day, according to Platts. US ethanol supply The US produced 16.4 billion gallons of ethanol in 2025, against an installed capacity of 18.5 billion gallons/year, leaving about 2 billion gallons of spare capacity, according to the study. US ethanol production capacity could expand to 18 billion-20 billion gallons/year by 2030 and 23 billion-26 billion gallons/year by 2035, supported by efficiency improvements, cellulosic production and new facilities, MEMA said. The study estimated that capturing 1% of international shipping’s fuel consumption with ethanol would require approximately 1 billion gallons annually, while a 5% share would require around 5 billion gallons annually. Ethanol, which has chemical and combustion properties similar to those of methanol, could generally be used in engines designed to run on methanol. The methanol-fueled fleet is expanding, with 157 vessels in service and more than 160 on order as of October 2026, according to S&P Global Maritime Portal data cited in the report. “Ethanol is moving beyond pilots, and this study shows the United States has the production base and export infrastructure to supply shipping at scale,” Global Centre for Green Fuels Managing Director Clarence Woo said in a statement. A.P. Moller-Maersk, one of the largest container lines, has been testing ethanol and ethanol-methanol blends in its methanol-capable fleet, progressing from a 10% ethanol blend to E100. On Sept. 28, the company’s 9,000 twenty-foot-equivalent-unit container ship, Tangier Maersk, completed the first commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of US corn ethanol in Houston. Kirby Corp. transported and bunkered the fuel. Regulatory uncertainty Regulatory uncertainty remains over the treatment of crop-based ethanol, although the International Maritime Organization has made progress toward recognizing specific production pathways. In May, the IMO agreed to include Brazilian second-crop corn ethanol in its draft revised lifecycle GHG assessment guidelines. The UN agency is still considering how indirect land-use change should be accounted for in other types of ethanol. Paula Nava, director of sustainability at Marquis Energy, a US ethanol producer, told Platts that IMO regulators should take fuel availability and existing national standards into consideration when defining sustainability criteria. “We should have a more flexible approach to what sustainability criteria is about,” Nava said. Under FuelEU Maritime, conventional crop-based ethanol continues to face less favorable regulatory treatment than advanced biofuels. “The next challenge is consistency,” Woo said, calling for standardized marine fuel specifications, traceable feedstocks and robust chain-of-custody systems. MEMA’s members include Bunker Holding, Raizen, Longi and Idemitsu, among other fuel producers, shipowners, ports, engine makers and classification societies. Source: Platts 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Future Fuel Talks: Predictable pricing can make blue ammonia more attractive to shipowners – NH3 Clean Energy
articles.summary: Long-term price certainty could give blue ammonia an advantage in a market where shipowners must weigh the cost of switching fuels against the emissions reductions they can achieve, Charles Whitfield told ENGINE. Charles Whitfield is the chairman of Australian clean ammonia developer NH3 Clean Energy. The company is...
articles.body: Future Fuel Talks: Predictable pricing can make blue ammonia more attractive to shipowners – NH3 Clean Energy in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 Long-term price certainty could give blue ammonia an advantage in a market where shipowners must weigh the cost of switching fuels against the emissions reductions they can achieve, Charles Whitfield told ENGINE. Charles Whitfield is the chairman of Australian clean ammonia developer NH3 Clean Energy. The company is developing a blue ammonia facility in Western Australia’s Pilbara region, with an initial production capacity of 650,000 mt/year targeted from 2030. Whitfield estimates the company could sell ammonia at $600/mt free on board (FOB) at Dampier without relying on Australian government subsidies. “There’s no subsidy. There’s nothing assumed in that price,” he said. Central to this pricing proposition is Western Australia’s domestic gas reservation policy. The policy requires LNG exporters to make gas equivalent to 15% of their exports available to the domestic market. Access to locally sourced natural gas through long-term bilateral contracts could allow NH3 Clean Energy to offer ammonia prices indexed to Australia’s consumer price index, rather than exposing them directly to oil-linked gas prices in the Middle East or Henry Hub-linked prices in the US, Whitfield explained. “In terms of a price proposition, it’s actually pretty attractive to a lot of customers who want to be able to secure long-term price security.” The $600/mt estimate excludes the cost of delivering ammonia to vessels. Whitfield expects the additional cost of bunker vessel deliveries within Dampier and nearby Port Hedland to be minimal due to the ammonia being already at the port. Deliveries to more distant markets such as Singapore and Japan could incur higher transport costs. To Pilbara and beyond NH3 Clean Energy and Pilbara Ports Authority plan to establish ammonia bunker operations by 2030. That date depends mainly on when production starts, not on building new port infrastructure, Whitfield said. “One of the great things about Dampier is that it already handles ammonia. There’s actually been a grey ammonia plant in the Burrup, which is the peninsula where Dampier Port is, for about 25 years,” he said. “There is a bulk liquid wharf with ammonia rundown lines, which is underutilised at the moment. It’s only operating at about 30% of its capacity, so actually we’re very fortunate that the infrastructure is already there.” The proposed production facility would sit about 20 kilometres south of Dampier. A pipeline would connect it to additional ammonia storage near the port, with existing infrastructure used to transfer the fuel to the wharf for loading onto bunker vessels. The region has already hosted an early ammonia bunker operation. CMB.TECH recently bunkered its bulk carrier Mineral Europa with green ammonia at Port Hedland using the bunker vessel Shenghang Yongle. The bulk carrier is currently chartered by Australian mining firm Fortescue. Bunker vessels can supply ships at both Dampier and Port Hedland, removing the need for separate ammonia storage facilities in Port Hedland. Early trials can also help develop the operating procedures, licensing arrangements and regulatory frameworks needed for routine ammonia deliveries in Pilbara, Whitfield said. NH3 Clean Energy is collaborating with Oceania Marine Energy on the design of an ammonia bunker vessel, which Oceania has said it plans to order. On the demand side, the company has secured non-binding offtake arrangements with Japan’s Mitsui OSK Lines and Itochu which are back-to-back demand aggregation agreements. Beyond the Pilbara, NH3 Clean Energy sees potential to supply major Asia-Pacific ports as the conflict in the Middle East creates uncertainty over ammonia prices and availability. Around 85% of Asia’s ammonia imports come from the Middle East, Whitfield said. Whitfield believes Western Australia’s location could offer a logistical advantage by allowing shipments to reach overseas markets without passing through major maritime chokepoints. He estimated that transporting ammonia from the Pilbara to Japan would cost half as much as from the Middle East and one-third as much as from the US. More than shipping Ships are only one part of NH3 Clean Energy’s intended customer base. The company expects to allocate around 20% of its initial production capacity to marine fuel. That would amount to approximately 130,000 mt/year, although the final allocation will depend on demand. The balance could be sold to power generation customers in Japan and Singapore or to established ammonia markets, including fertilisers, chemicals and other sectors. “There’s sort of three different markets that we address which helps us to diversify our customer base,” he said. “The speed of uptake of ammonia demand for shipping is still a little bit unknown. Obviously, the IMO outcome and a whole load of other variables will determine how much supply is required at certain stages. The way we mitigate that risk is essentially by addressing multiple markets.” Whitfield expects IMO member states to reach an agreement on the Net-Zero Framework in December, but believes it could be less stringent than the version approved in April 2025. “But I think that there will be a piece of paper or an agreement that does actually get ratified.” Carbon intensity over colour Blue ammonia is excluded from Australia’s hydrogen production tax incentive because of its fossil-based production pathway. Technology-specific eligibility requirements could also limit access to other government funding programmes. Whitfield suggested that a more technology-neutral approach, with incentives linked to lifecycle emissions reductions rather than production methods, could help scale uptake of the fuel. Low-emission fuels should be assessed on their actual greenhouse gas (GHG) performance rather than whether they are labelled blue or green, he said. NH3 Clean Energy expects to capture 99.5% of process emissions at its proposed facility, and Whitfield put its production emissions at 0.37 kgCO2/kg ammonia. The estimate does not establish the fuel’s full well-to-wake emissions intensity, which would also need to account for relevant upstream and onboard emissions. “You can talk about perfection, and it never happens, or you can actually get somewhere that is 97% of perfection and do that today. So it’s like, what do you want to do? Talk about it for 10 years or actually make it happen today?” he said. The distinction between production methods and emissions performance also has commercial implications. Whitfield said customers are increasingly concerned with emissions intensity because of regulations, GHG pricing and Scope 3 reporting requirements. Many are willing to pay a premium for emissions reductions rather than judging a fuel solely by whether it is labelled blue or green. Currently, the cost of renewable electricity and the efficiency of electrolysers remain significant obstacles to green hydrogen production. But NH3 Clean Energy could eventually replace blue hydrogen with green hydrogen in its ammonia production process if renewable electricity and electrolysis become commercially competitive, he added. “We would produce green tomorrow if there was a market for it,” he said. Expansion is also under consideration, both within the Pilbara and in other regions. “We are certainly looking to expand in the Pilbara because one of the things about blue ammonia is there aren’t actually that many places in the world where you can do it. You need plentiful gas supply, CCS [carbon capture and storage] sequestration capacity and access to market.” “And so, if you look around the world at where most of the blue ammonia plants have been built, it’s the Middle East, the US Gulf Coast and then the North West Shelf of Australia. There are a couple of other places, but I’m not going to give it away at this point in terms of where our sort of next ports of call are,” he said. “But yeah, one is obviously you’ve got to have market demand, but for blue especially, there are certain pieces of the jigsaw that you need to have in place.” Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/ 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

WASS previously secured a contract to supply torpedoes to the Indian Navy, strengthening its position in the country’s naval defence sector. The latest agreement builds on that presence by examining opportunities for broader industrial cooperation. However, the MoU does not constitute a confirmed manufacturing contract. articles.body: India plans five shipbuilding clusters to attract global players, target top 5 by 2047 in Shipbuilding News 19/11/2026 India is looking to attract global shipbuilders and shipping companies to develop five greenfield shipbuilding clusters across Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha and Tamil Nadu, as it seeks to rank among the world’s top 10 shipbuilding nations by 2030 and top five by 2047. At the India Shipbuilding Investment Conclave 2026 on Monday, minister for ports, shipping and waterways Sarbananda Sonowal said the government was working with the five coastal states to develop integrated shipbuilding ecosystems spanning vessel construction, repair, recycling and ancillary industries. The conclave saw participation from global and domestic maritime players, including HD Hyundai, Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, ABB Ship Management, Samsung Heavy Industries, Swan Defence and Heavy Industries, a Norwegian consortium and Hanwha Shipping. Several global and Indian shipping majors also expressed interest in having vessels built in India during an open-house interaction, signalling growing interest in the country’s shipbuilding ambitions. The government aims to build annual shipbuilding capacity of around 4.5 million gross tonnes by 2047, backed by a maritime investment package of approximately $8 billion. The package includes the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Scheme, Maritime Development Fund and Shipbuilding Development Scheme, which are intended to provide financial support, long-term capital and common infrastructure. India’s current shipbuilding capacity is just over 0.1 million gross tonnes, as per government and industry data. “Shipbuilding is central to this journey,” Sonowal said, adding that the industry would create opportunities across steel, engineering, electronics, marine equipment, design, logistics and maritime services. A $24 billion demand pipeline To give investors greater demand visibility, the government has identified requirements for more than 430 vessels across public-sector enterprises in different sectors. These represent a potential investment opportunity of nearly $24 billion for shipyards and equipment manufacturers, providing a prospective domestic demand pipeline, according to Sonowal. India’s existing shipbuilding order pipeline comprises more than 150 vessels valued at over $1.7 billion, with more than 80% of the order value coming from exports, the minister said. Orders from global shipping companies such as CMA CGM for emerging-fuel and dual-fuel LNG vessels indicate growing confidence in Indian shipyards. The five greenfield clusters will be developed through dedicated special purpose vehicles (SPVs), backed by central and state government incentives. Investors will be offered ready land on long-term leases under a plug-and-play model, supported by common marine infrastructure, utilities, connectivity and an institutional framework. The coordinated approach is intended to reduce project risks and shorten the time between investment decisions and the start of production. The government will also focus on specialised skill development to build a workforce for high-value shipbuilding and marine manufacturing. Sonowal cited global shipbuilding major HD KSOE’s proposed mega greenfield shipyard at Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu and capacity expansion investments of more than $1 billion by existing Indian shipyards as signs of growing investor confidence. Recycling to link with construction The government also plans to link ship recycling with new vessel construction through the Ship Recycling Credit Note Scheme. The scheme is intended to encourage shipowners to recycle end-of-life vessels at environmentally compliant Indian yards and use the resulting credits towards ordering new vessels from domestic shipyards. The minister also launched the Nau-kosh Indian Shipbuilding Portal, a digital platform that brings together government policies, approvals and investment opportunities to simplify access to information and improve ease of doing business. Emphasizing the importance of global partnerships, Sonowal urged international shipbuilders to partner with cluster SPVs, marine equipment manufacturers to establish local production and supply chains, and shipping lines to place repeat orders for technologically advanced vessels. articles.title: COSCO port fuels growth in APEC trade
articles.summary: As leaders and delegates focus on advancing regional economic integration under the framework of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a transformative megaproject on the eastern Pacific coast stands as a powerful testament to these shared goals. articles.body: COSCO port fuels growth in APEC trade in Port News 19/11/2026 As leaders and delegates focus on advancing regional economic integration under the framework of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a transformative megaproject on the eastern Pacific coast stands as a powerful testament to these shared goals. Chancay Port in Peru, a vital APEC economy, has rapidly evolved into a pivotal logistics hub connecting Latin America with Asia, breathing life into the vision of a seamlessly interconnected Asia-Pacific. Inaugurated in November 2024, the port was hailed by Chinese President Xi Jinping as the starting point of an Inca Trail of the New Era. Nearly two years into its operation, this flagship Belt and Road Initiative project — majority-owned by China’s COSCO Shipping — has turned that grand vision into a tangible reality. By slashing the one-way maritime transit time between Peru and China from roughly 35 days to just 23 days, the deep-water port has reduced logistics costs by more than 20 percent, fundamentally reshaping trans-Pacific trade dynamics. The $3.5 billion smart port has not only revolutionized Peru’s foreign trade, but also catalyzed economic integration across the broader Latin American region. With the launch of new feeder services like the Chancay Express Service 3 — known as CHX3 — which links Peru with Costa Rica, Chancay’s reach now extends to neighboring countries such as Brazil, Ecuador, Colombia and Chile. Carlos Aquino, director of the Center for Asian Studies at Peru’s National University of San Marcos, said that if Brazil routes its cargo through Chancay to China, it could save upwards of 15 days in transport time, highlighting the port’s immense geopolitical and economic magnitude. Over the past two years, the port has generated $3.65 billion in import and export trade, handling half a million twenty-foot equivalent units of containers. It is projected to bring $4.5 billion in annual economic benefits to Peru and create over 8,000 direct jobs. Furthermore, new direct shipping routes linking Chancay with major Chinese logistics hubs — including Shanghai, Guangzhou in Guangdong province and Nanjing in Jiangsu province — have established a comprehensive maritime network. A dedicated postal route for cross-border e-commerce has also been launched, cutting delivery lead times by over 20 days and offering a cost-effective solution for mass consumer products. Beyond macroeconomics, the “From Chancay to Shanghai” shipping link has profoundly transformed the lives of local entrepreneurs. At the just-concluded China International Import Expo in Shanghai, Peruvian artisans showcased handmade alpaca figurines and exclusive blueberry jams. Santusa Ansia Mamani Vilca, an indigenous weaver, said that the port has empowered local women by providing them with a direct channel to the vast Chinese market, thereby raising household incomes and preserving traditional culture. “Even tiny consignments now stand a chance to be showcased to Chinese buyers,” said Wang Bin, general manager of COSCO Shipping Ports Chancay Peru. Setting a benchmark for modern infrastructure, Chancay operates as South America’s first smart and green port. Powered entirely by green electricity, the facility boasts zero carbon emissions during operations. It utilizes artificial intelligence, digital twin technology and the internet of things to achieve 24/7 automated cargo processing. This commitment to sustainable development perfectly aligns with APEC’s agenda for green growth and digital innovation. The physical infrastructure is complemented by deepening institutional and cultural ties. The recently upgraded China-Peru Free Trade Agreement has further streamlined customs procedures, while cultural exchanges have fostered profound mutual understanding, making the port a true bridge of civilizations. As the Asia-Pacific community continues to champion open trade and mutual prosperity, Chancay Port stands as a shining example of what collaborative development can achieve. By bridging the geographical divide, this modern maritime artery is forging a resilient, inclusive and prosperous future for the entire Asia-Pacific region. articles.body: Asyad Group Operates New Integrated Trade Corridor Via Duqm Port To Gulf Markets in Port News 19/11/2026 Asyad Group, the global provider of integrated logistics services, announced the start of operational operations of the Green Corridor linking Duqm to Khalifa Port, in a step that enhances trade connectivity between the Sultanate of Oman and the United Arab Emirates, and opens wider horizons for the smooth movement of goods across regional markets. The corridor is witnessing a regular weekly flow of shipments through Asyad Container Terminal at Duqm Port, with expectations of growth in handling volumes during the next stage, enhancing the port’s role as a strategic gateway for regional trade, and supporting the integration of transport networks and logistics services between the Sultanate of Oman and Gulf markets. The Duqm – Khalifa Port Green Corridor was designed to provide an integrated trade route combining container handling and land transport within an interconnected operational system, through which goods arriving at Duqm Port move via the Khatmat Milahah border crossing to Al Ain Dry Port, reaching Khalifa Port in Abu Dhabi, and then connecting to distribution networks extending to various markets of the Gulf Cooperation Council countries. These operations are integrated with a coordinated cross-border customs system, contributing to facilitating transit procedures and reducing the periods goods remain at handling and transit points, which enhances the efficiency of trade flows and provides cargo owners with more flexible options in managing shipping and distribution operations, in addition to supporting the efficiency of using operational resources and improving the smooth movement of goods between markets. With the regularity of weekly shipment flows through Asyad Container Terminal in Duqm, and expectations of growth in their volumes during the next stage, the corridor enhances the role of Duqm Port as a strategic logistics gateway on global trade lines linking East and West, benefiting from its strategic geographical location and its advanced infrastructure and technical and operational capabilities qualifying it to receive large vessels and handle containers efficiently, in addition to its connection to regional transport, logistics services and distribution networks. Al Khattab bin Salim Al Maani, Vice President for Commercial Affairs at Asyad Ports and Free Zones, explained that global trade is witnessing rapid transformations imposing increasing requirements on supply chain flexibility, operations integration and speed of access to markets. The Duqm – Khalifa Port Green Corridor comes to enhance the trade connectivity system that Asyad Group is working to develop, by combining the operational capabilities of ports and land transport networks and cross-border logistics solutions, pointing out that this route has witnessed growing demand for it, reflecting the importance of providing integrated and flexible transport solutions that respond to the requirements of partners and cargo owners, and open wider horizons for trade between the Sultanate of Oman and Gulf markets. He said in a statement to Oman News Agency: This trend is not limited to the Duqm – Khalifa Port Green Corridor, but comes within a growing network of integrated trade corridors that Asyad Group launched during the past period to link Omani ports to regional markets. He added that this network includes green corridors for connectivity from Duqm Port to a number of Gulf markets, including Qatar and Saudi Arabia, in addition to the green corridors developed by the Group from Sohar Port to link the Sultanate of Oman to Gulf markets. He pointed out that this network reflects the integration of port infrastructure with land transport networks and cross-border logistics and customs solutions, providing multiple and flexible options for trade movement. Al Khattab bin Salim Al Maani affirmed that Asyad Group continues to develop an integrated network of trade corridors linking Omani ports to maritime shipping lines, land transport networks and regional markets, enhancing supply chain connectivity and consolidating the Sultanate of Oman’s position as a regional and global logistics hub, in line with the targets of Oman Vision 2040 aimed at enhancing the contribution of the logistics sector to economic diversification, and raising the readiness of the Sultanate of Oman to keep pace with transformations in global trade movement. articles.title: Coal is back: Which German power plants are the biggest winners from the energy crisis?
articles.summary: Germany’s thermal generation mix is shifting as stronger coal economics reshape plant profitability and dispatch. Kpler Insight identifies the units benefiting most, how their generation responds to changes in residual demand, and whether coal’s growing advantage can continue through winter. Key takeaways • Coal...
articles.body: Coal is back: Which German power plants are the biggest winners from the energy crisis? in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 Germany’s thermal generation mix is shifting as stronger coal economics reshape plant profitability and dispatch. Kpler Insight identifies the units benefiting most, how their generation responds to changes in residual demand, and whether coal’s growing advantage can continue through winter. Key takeaways • Coal gains competitiveness: High power prices, driven by elevated gas prices resulting in stronger clean dark spreads have supported a 10% y/y increase in German coal generation during Q3 2026. This is despite residual demand falling 4.3 GW, while gas output declined 8%, with a similar shift towards coal continuing into October YTD. • Profitability and dispatch shift: Stronger coal economics pushed hard-coal and lignite units ahead of gas in estimated benchmark profitability, with only one gas unit among the top 30 most profitable plants and Datteln 4 leading Q3 2026, while coal took a greater role in meeting residual demand, reshaping Germany’s thermal dispatch. • Winter outlook: Strong coal economics and substantial scheduled availability through Q1 2027 support continued coal dispatch, although low Rhine levels and existing coal-delivery restrictions remain the main near-term risks to generation. Stronger dark spreads reshape Germany’s thermal generation mix German coal generation increased in Q3 2026 as improving clean dark spreads widened coal’s economic advantage over gas, continuing the shift towards coal in the thermal mix over recent quarters. Despite residual demand falling 4.3 GW y/y in Q3, coal generation increased 10%, led by hard coal, while gas output declined 8%. The shift was primarily driven by elevated gas prices, which strengthened coal’s competitiveness against gas. Clean dark spreads turned positive at 8.4 €/MWh, with profitable hours increasing from 35% to 64% of the quarter, while clean spark spreads weakened to -21.4 €/MWh, with positive-spread hours declining from 51% to 48%. Hard coal and lignite overtake gas in benchmark profitability The shift was also evident at the unit level. Gas plants lead estimated net benchmark-margin rankings in Q3 2025, however, hard-coal and lignite units have since overtaken them in Q3 2026. Kpler Insight estimates show that gas units led Q3 2025 net benchmark margins at €119.9m, followed by hard coal at €27.8m, while lignite recorded -€62m, based on 36% coal/lignite and 54% gas efficiency assumptions. However, these estimates remain sensitive to efficiency assumptions, particularly for lignite, where margins ranged from ∼-€110m to €153m under the 32–42% efficiency range. By Q3 2026, lignite led with €458m in benchmark margins, followed by hard coal, which increased more than ninefold to €253.8m, overtaking gas, which declined 33% to €80.8m. Although estimated margins vary with plant efficiency assumptions, combined coal and lignite margins ranged from approximately −46% to +53% relative to the base estimate, compared with €9–171m for gas, reinforcing coal’s stronger economic position across different efficiency levels. Methodology: Net benchmark margins = hourly generation × (day-ahead price − estimated SRMC), including negative contributions. Base efficiency assumptions are 36% for hard coal and lignite (32–42% sensitivity range) and 54% for gas (50–60% sensitivity range). Estimates exclude plant-specific state subsidies and support payments, which could affect actual profitability At the technology level, the benchmark-margin rankings show a clear shift from gas to coal and lignite: • Q3 2025: Gas dominated the top 30 units, accounting for 21 gas, 7 hard-coal and 2 lignite units. • Q3 2026: Coal and lignite occupied 29 of the top 30 positions, split between 9 hard-coal and 20 lignite units, with GuD Herne 6 the only gas unit remaining. At the unit level: • Q3 2025: Gas units GuD Herne 6, Irsching 5 and Emsland D led the benchmark-margin rankings. • Q3 2026: Datteln 4 topped the rankings, followed by Lippendorf R, Neurath G and Walsum 10, highlighting the shift towards coal and lignite profitability. The trend continued into October YTD, with hard-coal and lignite benchmark margins increasing by 280–630% y/y, while gas margins declined 79%. Only two gas units, Irsching 5 and Irsching 4, ranked among the top 30 estimated benchmark-margin contributors, while GuD Herne 6 fell to 32nd place. Changing dispatch patterns highlight unit-level responsiveness In Q3 2026, coal generation increased by an estimated 293 MW for every 1 GW rise in residual demand, compared with 132 MW for gas, representing declines of 12% and 30% y/y, respectively. Coal continued to provide a larger incremental response than gas, although both became less sensitive to residual-demand changes y/y, potentially reflecting stronger coal economics supporting more consistent generation during lower residual-demand periods and limiting the additional output required as residual demand increased. Within the coal fleet, hard coal showed stronger alignment with residual demand, with R² rising from 0.63 to 0.71, while lignite declined from 0.74 to 0.58, suggesting that hard coal increasingly tracked residual-demand movements, whereas lignite followed a more stable, baseload-like generation profile. At the unit level, • Hard coal: Kraftwerk Rostock, Walsum 10 and Datteln 4 showed stronger residual-demand tracking, with Datteln 4 recording the largest improvement among the three. • Lignite: Schwarze Pumpe B and Lippendorf R became more responsive, while Neurath G and Boxberg Q showed weaker relationships despite stronger coal economics. • Gas: Herdecke H6 and KMW 3 showed the strongest relationships among gas units, while GuD Herne 6 and Irsching 5 weakened compared with Q3 2025. Outlook: Strong Coal Economics Support Winter Dispatch? Kpler Insights expects coal to remain significantly more profitable than gas through November and December, supported by elevated gas prices. Under 36% coal and 54% gas efficiency assumptions, clean dark spreads average 85 €/MWh in November and 72 €/MWh in December, compared with clean spark spreads of 6 €/MWh and -6.8 €/MWh, respectively, strongly favouring coal-fired generation. At unit level, most leading coal and lignite benchmark-margin contributors retain substantial scheduled availability through Q1 2027, including Datteln 4 (hard coal), Lippendorf R (lignite), Neurath G (lignite) and Walsum 10 (hard coal). Coal availability also improves into December, with Boxberg Q (lignite) rising from 744 MW to 893 MW and Lünen Trianel (hard coal) from 283 MW to 754 MW. However, Kpler model central hard-coal forecast remains 1 GW below EEX schedules in November and 1.7 GW below in December, highlighting uncertainty around effective availability. Rhine logistics remain the main near-term risk, particularly for inland coal units. BfG forecasts renewed low-water conditions during Week 45, while reported fuel-delivery restrictions at Walsum 10 and Grosskraftwerk Mannheim could limit dispatch despite favourable margins. Kpler’s Dry Bulk team expects an average $5/t discount to ARA coal prices in November, although higher inland freight costs could offset some of the benefit. Operators may also face incentives to conserve coal stocks for later delivery periods, but this remains a potential response rather than a confirmed strategy. articles.body: Americas Offshore Paratus and Vantris explore sale of Brazilian subsea venture Bojan Lepic November 19, 2026 0 21 1 minute read Seagems Seagems Paratus Energy Services and Malaysia’s Vantris Energy are looking into a potential sale of their jointly owned Brazilian subsea services business, Seagems, as part of a strategic review. The two companies, which each hold a 50% stake in Seagems, said they are jointly assessing third-party interest in acquiring the business as a whole. Seagems owns and operates six multipurpose pipelay support vessels (PLSVs), all currently working under contracts offshore Brazil. The review comes shortly after Seagems secured a four-year contract worth approximately $410m from Petrobras for the Seagems Safira pipelay support vessel. The newbuild is scheduled to begin operations offshore Brazil in late 2028. Paratus has meanwhile narrowed its focus to the Brazilian subsea market following the completion of the sale of its Mexican jackup drilling business in July. Both companies stressed that the strategic review may not result in a transaction and that neither partner has decided to sell the business. However, Paratus has appointed Pareto Securities as its financial adviser, while Vantris has engaged J.P. Morgan to make a more informed decision. articles.title: AlloySelect relaunches at Offshore Energy 2026 with new CCS screening preview
articles.summary: Originally developed by OGC Energy in 2018, AlloySelect is now being relaunched with enhanced corrosion assessment and materials selection capabilities, alongside a new CCS module designed specifically for CO2 transport and storage applications.
articles.body: Branded Content November 19, 2026 · 30 minutes ago AlloySelect relaunches at Offshore Energy 2026 with new CCS screening preview Originally developed by OGC Energy in 2018, AlloySelect is now being relaunched with enhanced corrosion assessment and materials selection capabilities, alongside a new CCS module designed specifically for CO2 transport and storage applications. Written in partnership with OGC Energy 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email OGC Energy The decisions behind the material Before engineers choose a material, they need confidence in the conditions against which it is being selected. Temperature, pressure, CO2, H2S, water chemistry and expected operating life all influence the assessment. A change in one assumption can alter the corrosion estimate, the materials shortlist or the level of further engineering required. That challenge is familiar to oil and gas projects. It is also increasingly relevant to carbon capture and storage (CCS), where engineers must consider the composition of transported CO2 streams, impurity specifications and the implications for equipment, pipelines and storage infrastructure. The calculations matter, but so does the ability to explain what was assumed and why a screening decision was reached. Eight years of practical engineering experience OGC Energy first developed AlloySelect in 2018 to bring its corrosion and materials engineering experience into a practical digital tool. Since then, the platform has been used to support clients working through corrosion assessment and materials selection questions. Feedback from that use has informed its relaunch for a new phase of energy projects. The objective remains straightforward: make early-stage corrosion and materials decisions easier to explore, repeat and communicate without taking engineering judgement out of the process. The refreshed offering brings together Evaluate and Select, with a new CCS screening preview introduced at Offshore Energy Exhibition & Conference (OEEC) 2026 in Amsterdam. Evaluate: make the assumptions visible AlloySelect Evaluate helps engineers estimate CO2 corrosion rates and see how the selected operating conditions affect the result. The interface brings inputs and outputs together, including calculated pH, corrosion rate, inhibited corrosion rate, corrosion allowance and environmental severity classification. Saved results and batch processing support repeated assessments across different cases. This makes a practical impact at the beginning of a project. Instead of presenting a corrosion-rate number in isolation, an engineer can examine the assumptions behind it and use the result as a starting point for the wider materials and corrosion-control discussion. Select: screen materials against actual service conditions AlloySelect Select addresses a closely related question: is a material suitable for the specified environment? Users choose the service conditions and candidate material, and the tool provides a screening outcome against the relevant NACE MR0175/ISO 15156 basis, together with applicable notes and restrictions. Those evaluations, where required, remain part of project-specific engineering. A key advantage of AlloySelect CCS is that it will also serve as a central repository for CO₂ stream specifications, industry guidance and technical data generated through Joint Industry Projects (JIPs), bringing together information that engineers can use to support consistent, informed materials decisions. The result helps teams distinguish a potentially acceptable option from one that requires a different selection or additional consideration. That can make early conversations more focused, particularly when project data and design assumptions are still evolving. A screening result is not a substitute for a full specification review, procurement requirements or project-specific qualification. However, it provides an essential starting point, helping engineers identify potential risks early, focus subsequent assessments and make more informed materials decisions. New CCS preview: start with the CO2 stream The new AlloySelect CCS preview extends this engineering-led approach to CO2 transport and storage applications. The demonstrator lets users compare a CO2 stream and its operating conditions against a selected reference specification, review impurity limits and see where the composition warrants closer attention. It also provides rule-based advisories for potential acid-dropout concerns and materials screening. Importantly, these are early warnings rather than a final engineering approval. The CCS preview does not calculate full thermodynamic phase behaviour, acid-dropout quantities or corrosion rates. Those evaluations, where required, remain part of project-specific engineering. A key advantage of AlloySelect CCS is that it will also serve as a central repository for CO₂ stream specifications, industry guidance and technical data generated through Joint Industry Projects (JIPs), bringing together information that engineers can use to support consistent, informed materials decisions. Visitors can see the software in action at stand 2.200 , explore representative conditions and discuss how the tools could support their own projects. The team will also introduce the AlloySelect relaunch during the exhibition's Stage program on Wednesday, November 25. For information about the platform and to arrange a demonstration, visit alloyselect.com . AlloySelect: materials decisions made simple. Under a memorandum of understanding signed on Thursday, Samsung Heavy will serve as the exclusive shipbuilder and Tesser as the exclusive reactor partner for the project, with both companies working on vessel design, reactor integration and regulatory licensing. Samsung Heavy has been exploring nuclear propulsion and floating nuclear power generation, but the latest tie-up represents a move towards demonstrating the technology on an actual LNG trading route. No shipbuilding contract or firm delivery date has been announced, although the partners are targeting the early 2030s. articles.title: LOGISTEED to acquire Neovia Logistics in global expansion deal
articles.summary: Japan’s LOGISTEED has signed a definitive agreement to acquire US-based Neovia Logistics, strengthening its contract logistics operations across North America and Europe. The transaction will bring Neovia under LOGISTEED as a wholly owned subsidiary, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing...
articles.body: Japan’s LOGISTEED has signed a definitive agreement to acquire US-based Neovia Logistics, strengthening its contract logistics operations across North America and Europe. The transaction will bring Neovia under LOGISTEED as a wholly owned subsidiary, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions. The companies expect to complete the acquisition between January and March 2027. The agreement marks another step in LOGISTEED’s international expansion strategy. It aims to combine the group’s transport and forwarding network with Neovia’s contract logistics capabilities. Acquisition expands global logistics network Headquartered in Dallas, Texas, Neovia provides warehousing, inventory management, fulfilment, reverse logistics and other value-added services. The company serves customers across several industries, including automotive, industrial manufacturing, consumer goods and retail. Neovia reported consolidated revenue of US$607 million for 2025 and employed 5,779 people at the end of the year. Its operations are concentrated in North America and Europe, complementing LOGISTEED’s established presence in Japan and the wider Asia-Pacific region. According to LOGISTEED, the acquisition will allow its customers to access additional contract logistics services in Western markets. Meanwhile, Neovia’s customers are expected to benefit from LOGISTEED’s transportation, freight forwarding and logistics capabilities across Asia. The companies also intend to combine their operational expertise and digital technologies to improve service quality and productivity. Transaction expected to close in early 2027 The acquisition will be carried out through a reverse triangular merger involving Neovia and a newly established US acquisition subsidiary of LOGISTEED. Under this structure, Neovia will remain the surviving legal entity and become a wholly owned subsidiary of LOGISTEED. The agreement was signed on 18 November 2026, with closing planned for the first quarter of 2027. However, completion remains subject to regulatory clearances, including competition and foreign investment approvals in the United States, Europe and other relevant jurisdictions. The financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The proposed combination is expected to strengthen LOGISTEED’s position in international contract logistics while expanding the range of supply chain services available to customers across its global network.

articles.title: Previous Ukraine port calls could put ships in Black Sea firing line
articles.summary: Merchant ships could be targeted in the Black Sea because of previous visits to Ukrainian ports, even when their current voyages have no connection to Ukraine, according to new intelligence highlighting an expansion of Russia’s maritime targeting campaign, something employed earlier by the Houthis in the Red Sea....
articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Europe Operations Tankers Previous Ukraine port calls could put ships in Black Sea firing line Sam Chambers November 19, 2026 0 370 2 minutes read Screenshot: SKAI Screenshot: SKAI Merchant ships could be targeted in the Black Sea because of previous visits to Ukrainian ports, even when their current voyages have no connection to Ukraine, according to new intelligence highlighting an expansion of Russia’s maritime targeting campaign, something employed earlier by the Houthis in the Red Sea. British maritime security specialist Ambrey has established that five of the six merchant vessels attacked in Romanian and Bulgarian waters since November 13 had called at Ukrainian ports at least once during 2026. More concerning for shipowners, Ambrey believes there is a realistic possibility that targeting decisions extend beyond individual vessels to include the Ukrainian trading history of other ships operated by the same owner or manager. Four of the six vessels were struck by aerial drones near Romania’s Sulina anchorage, while two were attacked in Bulgarian waters, extending the threat well beyond Ukraine’s territorial waters. One example is the Somali-flagged general cargo ship Betul 8, which sank off Bulgaria on Monday. Ambrey reports that its last confirmed Ukrainian port call was on July 8, more than four months before the attack. All 12 crewmembers were rescued. The following day, the Liberian-flagged LPG carrier Gas Husky was struck off Bulgaria while carrying 3,400 tonnes of LPG from Egypt to Romania. All 19 Filipino crewmembers were rescued. On Thursday, Philippine authorities confirmed that two of the sailors suffered minor injuries. Manila is also considering extending maritime high-risk and warlike area classifications to the southwestern Black Sea. Ambrey’s findings suggest that screening vessels for war risks may increasingly require reviewing entire fleet trading histories rather than simply assessing a ship’s intended voyage. The security firm warns that further attacks in Romanian and Bulgarian waters are likely, with smaller vessels particularly vulnerable to catastrophic damage. The warning comes amid another escalation in attacks on ships, ports and energy infrastructure. Russia’s defence ministry claimed on Wednesday that its drones struck facilities at Ukraine’s Danube port of Izmail and an unidentified cargo ship heading towards Pivdennyi, allegedly carrying dual-use military equipment. Neither claim has been independently verified. Meanwhile, Ukraine confirmed overnight strikes against the Ilsky and Afipsky refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar region, hitting storage tanks and a processing unit respectively. The two facilities have a combined annual crude processing capacity of approximately 13m tonnes. The latest exchanges follow Ukrainian strikes that severely damaged the Kerch Strait Bridge, threatening to delay the reopening of the Sea of Azov to commercial shipping. articles.body: Middle East Operations Tankers Fresh tanker strike adds to bloody week in Hormuz Sam Chambers November 19, 2026 0 400 2 minutes read CENTCOM CENTCOM Another tanker has been struck in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest in an escalating series of attacks on merchant shipping that has left two seafarers missing and more than a dozen injured this week. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) issued a fresh warning overnight after receiving reports that an unidentified tanker was hit by a projectile in its engine room while sailing out of the strait on Wednesday evening. The incident occurred approximately six nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at 16.45 GMT. All crew were reported safe and accounted for, although the extent of the damage and any environmental impact remain unknown. The latest attack follows confirmation from Abu Dhabi’s ADNOC Logistics & Services that one of its tankers was struck on Tuesday evening, leaving one seafarer missing and 11 injured. Maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified the vessel as the Liberian-flagged product tanker Navig8 Messi , which was hit approximately 13 nautical miles north of Khasab. The vessel was reportedly attacked previously in August, when it was struck by a drone alongside another ADNOC-linked tanker, Tarif. The Navig8 Messi also features on Iran’s blacklist of vessels it considers non-compliant with its restrictions on Hormuz transits. “Our immediate priority is supporting the search and rescue effort, our crew and those affected,” ADNOC said in a statement. The incidents follow Monday’s double strike on the LPG carrier Tara Gas , which was abandoned after catching fire. One Indian seafarer remains missing from that attack, while two others were injured. The renewed assault on commercial shipping comes amid a fresh escalation in hostilities between Washington and Tehran. Iran launched drone attacks against American military facilities in Kuwait and Bahrain on Wednesday following US strikes against a Revolutionary Guards missile installation on Qeshm Island, overlooking the strait. Both Gulf states reported intercepting incoming attacks. The latest attacks come as Washington tightens its blockade of Iranian shipping, warning that vessels receiving Iranian-origin cargo through ship-to-ship transfers could also face interception and seizure, even if they have never called at an Iranian port. Updated guidance issued by US Naval Forces Central Command said ships taking cargo from vessels subject to the blockade may themselves be treated as attempting to evade it. Such ships could be stopped, boarded, diverted or captured, while those failing to comply with US military instructions risk the use of force, including disabling or destructive fire. The warning adds another layer of risk for tanker owners and charterers handling Iranian cargo through offshore transfers. Washington reinstated its blockade of Iranian ports and coastal areas on July 14 after an earlier agreement with Tehran collapsed. The US maintains that neutral commercial shipping can continue transiting Hormuz to and from non-Iranian ports, although vessels remain subject to inspection. The Joint Maritime Information Center continues to rate the regional maritime security threat as severe, warning of further hostile activity in the Gulf and the strait. The growing disconnect between freight rates and vessel prices, and the industry’s tendency to overlook what might go wrong, will be among the key talking points when dry bulk executives gather in Geneva next April, reckons Emily Koo of Hong Kong shipowner TCC Group. Koo, one of more than 50 shipowners to take the stage at Geneva Dry 2027, is concerned that the industry is becoming too focused on explaining freight market rallies through statistics rather than examining the underlying health of the shipping business. She questions how long owners can continue justifying the disconnect between earnings and asset values while “sweeping what might go wrong” under the rug. With vessel prices remaining elevated, Koo believes shipowners also need to reconsider how they approach expansion. “Growth does not only mean buying a ship,” she says. There are different ways owners can position themselves for growth in these market conditions she says, citing building stronger relationships instead of going it alone, and examining whether equity should be reallocated across segments as examples. “Prohibitive pricing makes it difficult for companies to go it alone,” she says. Koo is similarly cautious about the industry’s growing enthusiasm for technology, warning that the pursuit of efficiency in individual areas of a business risks obscuring the bigger picture. “I think technology may force us to consider only a snapshot of commercial performance,” she says. While digital solutions can help optimise specific operations, Koo believes shipping must be viewed as a complete service rather than a collection of individual performance indicators. That means maintaining a consistent approach throughout an organisation, from the shipowner and management team to the seafarers delivering the service aboard vessels. Koo is group managing director and fourth-generation custodian of Hong Kong’s TCC Group, whose origins date to 1917, when her great-grandfather Koo Chung-shui established the family shipping business in Shanghai. The group subsequently relocated its operations to Hong Kong, building a century-long reputation in dry bulk and tanker shipping. Her preference for looking beyond headline numbers also shapes what she hopes to take away from Geneva Dry. Rather than presentations dominated by familiar market data, she wants to hear how industry leaders interpret the challenges facing dry bulk shipping and how they intend to respond. Geneva Dry 2027 will bring together shipowners, charterers, traders and other stakeholders from across the global dry bulk and commodities markets next April. articles.body: COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry has secured a large industrial site in Tianjin for the development of a new shipbuilding and offshore engineering base. Tianjin COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry acquired the approximately 146-hectare site in the Lingang area of the Tianjin Port Free Trade Zone for RMB570 million on 16 November. The project has an estimated total investment of around RMB8.2 billion and forms part of COSCO Shipping Group’s expansion in northern China. New yard to build containerships and bulk carriers The planned facility will have a total building area of approximately 448,000 square metres. It will include two dry docks capable of handling 300,000-tonne-class vessels, three outfitting quays of the same class and a range of modern production facilities. The new yard will focus on the construction of large bulk carriers and containerships. The first vessels are expected to be delivered in 2029. According to the Tianjin authorities, the development is intended to support the growth of a complete regional shipbuilding supply chain. This will cover raw materials, vessel design, final assembly, equipment manufacturing, processing and maintenance services. The project is also expected to work alongside established shipbuilding and offshore engineering companies in the region, including Dalian Shipbuilding Industry’s Tianjin operations, Offshore Oil Engineering and BOMESC. Once it reaches full production capacity, the facility is expected to generate annual output of approximately RMB6 billion and support more than 5,000 jobs. The Lingang area already hosts an established marine equipment and offshore engineering cluster. Its industrial infrastructure includes deepwater waterfront access, heavy-equipment sites, port transport connections and support from the Tianjin Free Trade Zone. The Tianjin authorities said the new COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry base would add large-scale professional dock capacity and strengthen the region’s capabilities in high-end vessel assembly.

MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Transocean Equinor rig Source: Amplitude Energy Amplitude Energy, an Australian gas production company focused on supplying the Southeast domestic gas market, has kicked off drilling operations at an exploration well off the coast of Victoria, where a promising geological structure offers an 81% probability of geological success, as the company advances its East Coast gas project. After the drilling operations at the company’s Annie-2 well reached a total depth of 2,253 meters measured depth, the company said the data collected from the well confirmed excellent quality of the reservoir, indicating a significant improvement in permeability, porosity, and deliverability compared to the initial discovery .
