articles.title: Guinea storms into iron ore export top three
articles.summary: Guinea has overtaken South Africa to become the world’s third-largest seaborne iron ore exporter, with the rapid ramp-up of the giant Simandou project providing a fresh boost to long-haul capesize demand. New figures from shipping association BIMCO show Guinean iron ore shipments topped 5m tonnes for the first time...
articles.body: Africa Dry Cargo Guinea storms into iron ore export top three Adis Ajdin November 19, 2026 0 443 2 minutes read Star Bulk Star Bulk Guinea has overtaken South Africa to become the world’s third-largest seaborne iron ore exporter, with the rapid ramp-up of the giant Simandou project providing a fresh boost to long-haul capesize demand. New figures from shipping association BIMCO show Guinean iron ore shipments topped 5m tonnes for the first time in October, giving the West African country a 3% share of global seaborne volumes. More than 22m tonnes have been shipped so far this year, already surpassing earlier industry expectations of around 20m tonnes for the whole of 2026. The impact on shipping demand is proving far greater than the additional cargo volumes suggest. BIMCO shipping analysis manager Filipe Gouveia calculates that Guinean ore travels, on average, 88% farther than a typical seaborne iron ore shipment, with exports heading almost exclusively to China. That helped Guinea account for 6% of global iron ore tonne-mile demand in October, double its share by cargo volume. Growing shipments from the country also helped lift worldwide iron ore tonne-miles by 2% during the first ten months of 2026, despite little change in overall volumes. The figures add weight to the bullish outlook voiced by dry bulk owners at October’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco. Star Bulk’s Milena Pappas highlighted Guinea’s booming bauxite exports and the Simandou ramp-up as major drivers for capesize and newcastlemax demand. She suggested Simandou could ship 65m tonnes next year, well above earlier expectations of 45m tonnes. CTM chairman John Michael Radziwill went further, predicting a “generational rate rally” for the sector. BIMCO’s longer-term projections point to an even bigger shift in dry bulk trading patterns. If Simandou reaches its planned annual output of 120m tonnes without displacing existing exports, global iron ore tonne-mile demand could rise by 13% compared with 2025 levels. Even if the entire volume replaces shipments from established suppliers, the longer Guinea-China voyage would still generate a 6% increase in tonne-mile demand. How much of that growth reaches the conventional capesize market remains another question. Splash reported in August that shipbroker SSY had found vessels above 220,000 dwt accounted for nearly half of Simandou’s first-half shipments. With Chinese operators controlling a substantial share of the VLOC orderbook, a sizeable portion of the emerging trade could be tied up in dedicated tonnage rather than finding its way into the spot market. China Merchants Energy Shipping has already secured a 25-year transportation contract worth at least $2.8bn covering six VLOCs serving the Simandou trade. There is also uncertainty over how quickly the project can reach full capacity. Shipping analysts at Scandinavian bank SEB have pointed to differing timelines, with port and rail operator CTG expecting infrastructure capable of handling 120m tonnes annually by the end of 2027, while mining giant Rio Tinto has targeted full mine production in the second half of 2028. articles.summary: The global oil tanker fleet could expand by 45% and the LNG carrier fleet by 80% by 2050, according to new projections from the International Energy Agency (IEA), highlighting shipping’s continued dependence on fossil fuel trades even as the energy transition gathers pace. articles.body: Gas Tankers IEA sees tanker fleet expanding by 45% and LNG carriers by 80% by 2050 Sam Chambers November 19, 2026 0 285 1 minute read BW LNG BW LNG The global oil tanker fleet could expand by 45% and the LNG carrier fleet by 80% by 2050, according to new projections from the International Energy Agency (IEA), highlighting shipping’s continued dependence on fossil fuel trades even as the energy transition gathers pace. The figures feature in a new 55-page IEA study examining extreme weather risks to international energy shipping. Under the agency’s Current Policies Scenario, which assumes a relatively slow energy transition, oil and gas shipping activity is projected to rise from approximately 32trn tonne-kilometres today to 47trn by 2050. Even under its Stated Policies Scenario, which assumes faster improvements in energy efficiency and clean technology deployment, oil tanker fleet capacity requirements are projected to increase by 35%, with LNG carrier numbers rising 60%. The findings underline the continuing importance of tonne-mile demand in shaping tanker markets. Since 2000, seaborne crude oil volumes have grown by just 15%, but tanker transport activity measured in tonne-kilometres has increased by around 40%, reflecting the shift in refining capacity and oil import demand towards Asia. LNG volumes, meanwhile, have quadrupled over the same period. The IEA also highlights how climate-related disruptions could further stretch effective vessel supply A tanker sailing from the US Gulf to Japan via the Cape of Good Hope rather than the Panama or Suez canals would travel an additional 13,000 km, adding 26 days to the voyage and increasing fuel consumption by 75%. With weather-related port downtime projected to increase by 35% by mid-century, the report suggests that longer voyages, delayed cargoes and more frequent diversions could further tighten vessel availability and support freight rates. articles.summary: DP World has completed the latest expansion of its deep-water container terminal in Posorja, Ecuador, extending the berth to 800 metres and increasing annual handling capacity to 1.4 million TEU. articles.body: DP World has completed the latest expansion of its deep-water container terminal in Posorja, Ecuador, extending the berth to 800 metres and increasing annual handling capacity to 1.4 million TEU. The development forms part of a privately funded investment of more than US$200 million. It is intended to accommodate larger vessels, improve terminal efficiency and strengthen Ecuador’s connections with international markets. The latest work follows the completion of a 700-metre berth earlier in 2026. New cranes to enter service in 2027 DP World has also added a fully electric quay crane and three hybrid rubber-tyred gantry cranes at Posorja. The new quay crane is 56 metres high and has a reach of 72 metres. It can serve container vessels measuring up to 400 metres in length, with capacities ranging from 20,000 to 24,000 TEU. The crane can lift loads of up to 65 tonnes. The three hybrid yard cranes are expected to consume 40% less diesel than conventional equipment. DP World estimates that they will prevent more than 900 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually. The equipment is undergoing final preparations and is expected to enter service in early 2027. Once operational, Posorja will have seven quay cranes and 18 yard cranes. “This expansion is a significant investment in Ecuador’s trade competitiveness and long-term economic growth,” said Carlos Merino, CEO of DP World in Ecuador, Peru and Colombia. “By increasing capacity, accommodating larger vessels and introducing more efficient equipment, we are helping Ecuadorian businesses move goods more reliably and connect with international markets,” he added. Additional investment in reefer infrastructure DP World is also expanding infrastructure supporting Ecuador’s agricultural and seafood exports. The programme includes electric internal transfer vehicles and an approximately 50% increase in electrical connections for refrigerated containers. Further projects include a planned solar power facility and more than US$10 million in electrical infrastructure investment to improve energy supplies and operational reliability. DP World has invested approximately US$700 million in Posorja since the terminal began operating in 2019. The company said the terminal’s international connectivity has also expanded through the introduction of a direct container service between Ecuador and Asia.

articles.title: Freightos Weekly Update: US air cargo recovering from outage; new US-CN tensions ahead of talks
articles.summary: Air cargo networks in the US are recovering from the major disruption over the weekend. Though the air traffic control system failure grounded thousands of flights and is likely to cause some delays for air freight, international air rates to the US – which were already climbing on peak season demand for many lanes –...
articles.body: Air cargo networks in the US are recovering from the major disruption over the weekend. Though the air traffic control system failure grounded thousands of flights and is likely to cause some delays for air freight, international air rates to the US – which were already climbing on peak season demand for many lanes – have not surged significantly as a result. Freightos Air Index China – N. America prices increased 16% to $9.25/kg last week but have not climbed further since the outage. This rate is already well above 2025’s peak season high of $8.00/kg reached only in mid-December last year. Seasonal volumes are layering on top of already-elevated demand and tight space due to data center buildouts. Transatlantic rates climbed 12% to an average of $3.27/kg last week, and likewise have not moved significantly higher since the communications failure. Europe-US peak season demand is likely combining with Asia-origin volumes seeking space on alternative lanes to provide demand side pressure. Meanwhile, capacity reductions from winter schedules, and freighter shifts to higher volume lanes may also be helping push spot prices to their highest since December 2022. In ocean freight, container carriers continue to march back to the Red Sea on Asia-Europe lanes. Together with the rapidly growing global fleet, the Red Sea rebound increases the likelihood of an overcapacity challenge for carriers – and downward pressure on rates across lanes – next year. For now though, bolstered by lingering congestion and higher fuel costs, Asia – Europe container prices are 40% – 50% higher than a year ago. Asia – N. Europe rates were level at about $3,400/FEU last week and are down 5% compared to the end of October. Asia – Mediterranean prices were also about steady at $4,300/FEU. This stability shows that start of month GRIs did not succeed and suggest that plans for mid-month increases may also not take, though carriers are increasing blanked sailings during this demand lull, and labor strikes in France and Spain may help absorb some capacity. Carriers are announcing increases for December too, and these price bumps could be more likely to materialize if supported by pre-Lunar New Year demand. Transpacific rates are still at about at peak levels with prices ticking up slightly last week to $8,460/FEU to the West Coast and $9,850/FEU to the East Coast even as we enter the second half of November. Delays for containers moving inland by rail remain a problem at LA/Long Beach, even as the ILWU Local 26’s November 20th strike deadline approaches. President Trump is set to meet with China’s Xi Jinping this week with the interim China-US trade agreement set to expire on January 10th. Though the two states seemed set on a course for further deescalation and may still be most likely to take that path, multiple recent factors – the midterm elections, new faces and debates in the White House, the Nvidia scandal and new controls over Chinese access to advanced US chips – are creating more tension and less certainty around where the relationship goes from here. Finally, lower than normal rainfall in Panama over the summer triggered draft and daily transit restrictions for Panama Canal crossings, with container carriers rolling out surcharges for impacted lanes. Better than expected precipitation since then, however, has allowed the Panama Canal Authority now to reverse those steps. Even so, expectations for a coming El Nino could still mean that restrictions will be reintroduced in the coming months. But with current water levels about back to normal for this time of year, the latest projections downgrading the severity of the El Nino, and expectations that next year’s rainy season could be strong and start on time, the risk of severe disruptions from canal restrictions in Q4 and through the first half of 2027 may be lower now than feared over the summer. Judah Levine, Head of Research, Freightos Group (Nasdaq: CRGO)

articles.title: CEVA Logistics and SIT launch AI and robotics lab in Singapore
articles.summary: CEVA Logistics and the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) have opened a joint innovation laboratory in Singapore to develop robotics and artificial intelligence solutions for warehouse operations. The Intelligent Logistics & Autonomous Systems (ILAS) Lab forms part of a five-year collaboration between the two...
articles.body: CEVA Logistics and the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) have opened a joint innovation laboratory in Singapore to develop robotics and artificial intelligence solutions for warehouse operations. The Intelligent Logistics & Autonomous Systems (ILAS) Lab forms part of a five-year collaboration between the two organisations. The initiative will focus on automating repetitive warehouse tasks, including product assembly, labelling and packing. It aims to make these operations more flexible while reducing the time employees spend on manual activities. The laboratory is supported by the Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) and the National Robotics Programme (NRP). New technologies targeted for CEVA’s Blue Hub The collaboration will combine CEVA’s operational experience with SIT’s research capabilities in robotics, AI vision systems and connected automation. A particular focus will be on value-added services, where warehouses handle different products in relatively small batches. These operations are often difficult to automate because product sizes, packaging requirements and customer orders frequently change. At CEVA’s Blue Hub facility in Singapore, value-added services account for approximately half of all warehouse floor hours. The company plans to use the laboratory to develop automation systems that can adapt to these changing requirements. According to CEVA, solutions developed through the initiative are expected to be deployed at Blue Hub within the next one to two years. Before deployment, the technologies will undergo testing and operational trials to assess their performance and suitability. “The joint innovation lab is part of CEVA’s vision for the Warehouse of Tomorrow,” said Guy Meredith, Contract Logistics Vice President, APAC, CEVA Logistics. “Working with SIT, we aim to bring adaptable automation from applied research into everyday operations, helping our teams improve efficiency and respond to changing customer requirements,” Meredith added. The company also intends to assess whether successful applications could be introduced across other customer operations in its Asia Pacific network. Alongside technology development, the partnership will support research and training opportunities for SIT students. More than 130 SIT students and graduates have gained exposure to CEVA’s operations since 2023. The new laboratory will provide further opportunities to participate in applied research projects. The initiative builds on CEVA’s existing automation activities in Singapore, including its earlier pilot of autonomous electric vehicles at Blue Hub. The partners have not disclosed the financial value of the five-year collaboration.

articles.body: DHL Global Forwarding has introduced a dedicated air freight service connecting Hong Kong, Navi Mumbai and Liège, expanding its cargo network between China, India and Europe. The new route will operate twice weekly using a Boeing 747 freighter, with DHL Aviation providing the aircraft capacity. It marks DHL Global Forwarding’s first dedicated freighter service serving India. The connection will provide direct cargo capacity between Hong Kong and the Mumbai region. It will also support shipments from India to Europe through DHL’s network in Liège, Belgium. New service offers regular cargo capacity The Boeing 747 freighter provides approximately 100 tonnes of total aircraft capacity per flight. Initially, DHL Global Forwarding is targeting 25 to 30 tonnes of cargo per flight on the India sectors. This represents approximately 50 to 60 tonnes per week, with potential for further growth as demand increases. The service is designed to support companies shipping high-value and time-sensitive goods between Asia and Europe. Expected cargo includes pharmaceuticals, electronics, industrial machinery and precision components. DHL also expects demand from healthcare, engineering and advanced manufacturing customers. “India is a strategic market for DHL Global Forwarding and an increasingly important part of our global air freight network,” said Henk Venema, Global Head of Air Freight, DHL Global Forwarding. “With this new dedicated service, we are strengthening connectivity between China, India and Europe and providing our customers with reliable capacity and greater access to key growth markets,” Venema added. DHL plans further expansion in India The new connection forms part of DHL Global Forwarding’s wider plans to strengthen its presence in the Indian air freight market. The company is also planning a dedicated service between Bengaluru and Europe, with a targeted launch in March 2027. The additional route would provide further capacity for exporters and importers using India’s growing manufacturing and technology hubs. According to DHL, the expansion responds to increasing demand for dedicated air freight capacity as international trade and manufacturing activity develop. The company expects the new services to strengthen cargo connections between India and major European distribution markets.

articles.body: Everllence has secured its first order for the 8S50ME-GI Mk10.7 dual-fuel engine. The engines will power two new RoRo vessels ordered by European shipping operator CLdN. Each vessel will have a capacity of 6,700 lane metres and will be built by HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea. Hyundai EMD will manufacture the engines, with testing scheduled for July 2028. Delivery to the shipyard is expected in September 2028. The agreement follows CLdN’s earlier order for the two RoRo vessels, which are scheduled for delivery in 2029. New engines support dual-fuel operations The engines will use Everllence’s ME-GI technology, allowing the vessels to operate on methane or conventional fuel oil. According to the company, the technology offers high fuel efficiency and low methane slip. This provides operators with greater flexibility when selecting fuels. Both engines will also feature Everllence’s EcoEGR exhaust gas recirculation system. The technology is designed to meet IMO Tier III emissions requirements. The propulsion systems will use controllable-pitch propellers, supporting the operational requirements of the new RoRo vessels. “Choosing Everllence’s ME-GI engine for these vessels was a natural choice and extends a long-standing partnership,” said Cameron Bowie, COO Shipping, CLdN. “These engines will provide the vessels with a combination of outstanding fuel efficiency and the flexibility of dual-fuel propulsion,” Bowie added. The order represents the first commercial application of the S50-bore ME-GI engine on Everllence’s latest Mk10.7 platform. The engines will also offer the option to connect to the company’s CEON digital platform. This would allow operators to access remote monitoring, technical support and operational data. November 18, 2026 © Wangkun Jia - stock.adobe.com The U.S. Coast Guard awarded a $155 million contract to The Whiting-Turner Contracting Co., of Greenbelt, Maryland, to construct a new Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics facility at the U.S. Coast Guard Academy. The contract, awarded Nov. 16, is one month ahead of schedule and supports the Coast Guard’s ongoing effort to modernize Academy facilities and prepare future officers for service in a technologically advanced maritime environment. The approximately 120,000 square-foot facility, commonly known as STEM West, will include laboratories, classrooms and design spaces supporting the Academy’s engineering curriculum. It will serve as the future home of the Coast Guard’s chemistry; naval architecture and marine engineering; and civil and environmental engineering programs. The accelerated design-build-to-budget contract will incorporate stakeholder input as the final design is completed. Construction is expected to conclude in spring 2030. The STEM West award also marks a Coast Guard-wide milestone. The service has now obligated $20 billion of the nearly $25 billion in funding provided through the Working Families Tax Cuts Act. Separately, the Coast Guard awarded a $29.3 million contract Sept. 29 to Healtheon Inc., of New Orleans, to repair, renovate and reconfigure Waesche Hall. Funded through the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, the project is expected to be completed in May 2029. The Waesche Hall project will modernize approximately 40,000 square feet of the building’s 60,000-square-foot footprint. Planned work includes repairs to bathrooms, faculty offices, classrooms, high-density bookshelves and Admissions Department spaces. The project also includes reconfiguring the first-floor museum exhibit area to accommodate a projection screen and temporary foldable assembly seating. On the second floor, the renovation will add three classrooms, library space, offices and academic department spaces. The improvements will enhance areas used by cadets for collaboration and study, including dedicated space for teaching and learning. The projects are part of a broader Academy modernization effort that includes construction of a new aquatics center and parking garage, as well as improvements to cadet living conditions in Chase Hall. In August, the Coast Guard awarded a $51 million contract to renovate Chase Hall Annex A. Founded in 1876, the U.S. Coast Guard Academy is one of five federal service academies. Each year, approximately 200 graduates are commissioned as Coast Guard officers and begin serving in America’s multi-mission maritime military force.

articles.summary: Nine major shipping associations are urging governments to reach an agreement on global greenhouse gas regulations, warning that continued uncertainty threatens investment in cleaner ships and alternative fuels ahead of...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: BNMK 0819/Shutterstock Nine major shipping associations are urging governments to reach an agreement on global greenhouse gas regulations, warning that continued uncertainty threatens investment in cleaner ships and alternative fuels ahead of critical negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). The joint statement , issued Wednesday, calls for practical, enforceable and globally consistent rules that would give shipowners and fuel suppliers the certainty needed to invest in maritime decarbonization. The appeal comes as governments prepare to revisit the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, whose formal adoption was postponed in October 2025 amid opposition from the United States and several oil-producing countries. The framework, approved in draft form in April 2025, would combine progressively stricter greenhouse gas fuel-intensity requirements with a mechanism that places a price on certain emissions. The nine organizations—including BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERTANKO, INTERCARGO and the World Shipping Council (WSC)—reaffirmed their support for the IMO’s goal of achieving net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. However, they stressed that any agreement must account for the cost and availability of alternative fuels, provide flexible compliance mechanisms and avoid overlapping national and regional regulations. The statement stops short of explicitly endorsing the existing Net-Zero Framework in its current form, instead acknowledging that alternative government proposals remain under consideration. Industry Support Comes With Conditions The appeal follows a recent analysis by InfluenceMap that found broad industry support for a global IMO climate agreement, but significant differences over carbon pricing, fuel standards and how emissions from alternative fuels should be calculated. The London-based research organization found that industry support has become more cautious since the framework’s adoption was postponed last year. Before that decision, ICS and WSC had backed the proposed framework as is. More recently, shipping associations have emphasized reaching an agreement without explicitly endorsing the original package. Another point of contention is the relationship between global IMO rules and existing European regulations. Several shipping associations have called for reviewing or harmonizing the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime requirements once an international framework is established, arguing that overlapping regulations would impose unnecessary costs. Critical Negotiations Ahead The renewed industry push comes ahead of an IMO working group meeting November 23–27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s MEPC 85 session from November 30 to December 3. A previously adjourned extraordinary session could resume December 4 to consider adoption of the framework. Negotiators face deep divisions over carbon pricing, compliance costs and the treatment of different marine fuels. For shipowners making investment decisions on vessels expected to operate for decades, the outcome could shape everything from ship design to fuel procurement and infrastructure development. The industry groups say a global agreement is essential to maintaining a level playing field. Whether governments can deliver that certainty while preserving the emissions-reduction ambitions of the original framework remains an open question. (Screenshot from video) The LPG tanker TARA GAS remained on fire and adrift in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, according to a new navigational warning, as independently verified video showed the vessel engulfed in a massive blaze following repeated attacks that left one seafarer missing. The latest developments come as ADNOC Logistics & Services confirmed a separate attack on one of its tankers in the waterway, leaving another crew member missing and 11 injured. A NAVAREA IX navigational warning issued at 1500 UTC Wednesday identified TARA GAS as still burning and drifting southeast, approximately 5.7 nautical miles off Khawr Ghub Ali, Oman. Mariners were cautioned to avoid the disabled vessel. The warning provides the clearest indication yet that the fire continued into Wednesday, despite some reports suggesting it had been extinguished. Meanwhile, Reuters has independently verified dramatic footage circulating on social media showing TARA GAS engulfed in flames, with thick black smoke billowing above the vessel. The news agency confirmed the location using coastal landmarks, satellite imagery and topographical data, while matching the vessel’s superstructure and stern to archival photographs. NASA satellite fire-detection data also recorded thermal activity at the location on November 17. Reuters could not establish exactly when the footage was recorded. The Panama-flagged LPG tanker was initially attacked on November 16, approximately seven nautical miles north of Khasab, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) . The strike disabled the vessel and caused an engine-room fire. A subsequent attack on November 17 sparked another fire and forced the crew to abandon ship. Omani authorities rescued 24 of the vessel’s 25 crew members, while one Indian seafarer remains missing. India’s Ministry of External Affairs said two Indian crew members were hospitalized in Khasab. The attacks and rescue operations were detailed in gCaptain’s earlier reporting . In another significant development, ADNOC Logistics & Services confirmed Wednesday that one of its vessels was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on the evening of November 17. The company said one crew member remained unaccounted for, while the remaining crew had been evacuated. Eleven seafarers sustained injuries and were receiving medical care where required. “Our immediate priority is supporting the search and rescue effort, our crew and those affected,” ADNOC L&S said. The company did not identify the vessel. However, maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified it as the Liberian-flagged product tanker NAVIG8 MESSI , which is commercially managed by ADNOC L&S. A new time-late report from the UKMTO appears to correspond to the ADNOC incident. The report, based on information from local authorities, said a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile approximately 13 nautical miles north of Khasab on November 17. A fire broke out aboard the vessel but was subsequently extinguished. UKMTO said search-and-rescue efforts were continuing for one missing crew member, while the extent of the vessel’s damage and any environmental impact remained unknown. The warning did not identify the tanker by name. The reported attack on NAVIG8 MESSI would be the second against the vessel in recent months. ADNOC previously confirmed that two of its ships were targeted by drones in the Strait of Hormuz on August 13, with Vanguard identifying them as NAVIG8 MESSI and TARIF . No injuries were reported in those earlier incidents. The latest attacks underscore the continuing danger to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. articles.body: Ukrainian Drone Attacks Halve Russian Oil Refining in November Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Sunshine Seeds Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, according to estimates from two industry sources, as Kyiv ramps up strikes on energy infrastructure. Russia is already facing domestic fuel shortages in some regions and restricted ex port capacity due to crippling Ukrainian strikes on port s. Reduced refining could also tighten global fuel markets and hamper Russia's ability to deliver on a deal to ex port diesel to the United States. The attacks now have disrupted or halted operations at 15 of Russia's 35 major refineries, the two people said, up from 9 in the middle of last week. Russia's energy ministry did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. MOSCOW AND KYIV RAMPING UP STRIKES ON ENERGY TARGETS US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on October 11. Though neither Moscow nor Kyiv acknowledged agreeing to it and attacks continued, Ukrainian strikes did ease for roughly two weeks. The war has since intensified, however, with Ukrainian drone attacks increasing in scale and frequency as Russia ramps up its own drone and missile strikes. Ukraine hit a strategically im port ant bridge and targeted oil refineries this week in what Russian ‌defence ministry data showed on Monday was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of the war in 2022. Following near-daily drone strikes over the last 20 days, crude processing volumes at Russian refineries have fallen to around 400,000 metric tons per day, or around 3 million barrels per day, from over 700,000 metric tons per day at the end of October, the estimates showed. The combined nominal capacity of Russian refineries affected by the attacks since late October stands at around 500,000 tons per day, equivalent to approximately 54% of the country's total primary refining capacity of an estimated 930,000 tons per day. However, the sources said that, given the gradual reduction in operating capacity, average crude processing volumes in November remain above 500,000 tons per day, about 5% to 10% below September and October levels. Major Russian refineries affected by the attacks include plants in Ryazan, Yaroslavl, Kirishi and the Volga region, the people said. (Reuters)

That’s in addition to two ships laden with US fuel that turned sharply north toward Europe, diverting away from Asia, since last week. The diversions come amid weaker demand from some major buyers in Asia — where LNG prices have fetched a discount to Europe — and other regions, although global supplies remain tight because of continued disruptions in the Middle East. The LNG flows to Europe have helped curb prices there, after benchmark gas futures hit an almost four-year high last month. For Egypt, the recent price rallies made spot LNG purchases more expensive, and there have also been some capacity expansions scheduled to increase gas flows from Israel to Egypt, he said. Egypt’s cabinet earlier this month approved a rationing plan for power consumption that state bodies will implement during the current financial year to cope with the spillover effects of the Iran war. Egypt had to curb some electricity usage this year as it grappled with high fuel costs due to the conflict. The Al Qassar tanker, carrying US LNG, turned west away from Egypt earlier this week after reaching the country’s Port Said, according to ship-tracking data. Kpler estimates it’s now heading toward Europe. The Amaryllis Knutsen vessel, also loaded with US fuel, made a sharp U-turn on Tuesday near Egypt. Separately, there’s been a diversion from Egypt toward Asia recently, based on Kpler and data on Bloomberg, with the Greenergy Wind tanker turning south in the mid-Atlantic on Tuesday. It’s signaling the Cape of Good Hope, a usual route toward Asia. A sustained fall in LNG spot prices could prompt buyers in South and Southeast Asia to purchase more cargoes, especially as big importers remain on the sidelines, according to traders. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: US Cracks Down on Iran Oil Blockade, Threatening Action Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 © Adobe Stock/alones The US military will treat ships that receive cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran as attempting to evade its blockade of Iranian ports and could take action against them, according to an advisory issued by US Central Command (CENTCOM) on Wednesday. The US naval blockade on Iran-related oil exports was first imposed on April 13 and lifted in June after Washington reached a draft understanding with Tehran. It was reimposed on July 14 after the agreement collapsed. "Any ship that receives cargo via a ship-to-ship transfer with a vessel subject to the blockade and carrying cargo loaded at an Iranian port or coastline may be considered to be evading the blockade, even if it has not entered Iranian ports or the Iranian coastline," CENTCOM said in an update. "Such ships may be stopped, boarded, diverted, captured, or directed to proceed to the Iranian port where the cargo originated." Ships that fail to comply immediately with lawful orders from blockade or boarding forces could face enforcement action, "including the use of force consistent with applicable law", the advisory added. Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite the US naval blockade, according to shipping intelligence and security sources who spoke to Reuters in October. Iran's crude exports, however, have remained near a standstill for months, shipping sources say. (Reuters)

The towboat rolled to starboard after being struck and later capsized and sank, killing one crewmember. (Source: NTSB/U.S. Coast Guard) A Houston ship pilot has been indicted on a federal seaman’s manslaughter charge over a deadly 2024 collision in the Houston Ship Channel, in what federal officials describe as the first prosecution of its kind involving a ship pilot. Darris Ornel Jefferson, 39, is accused of misconduct, negligence and inattention to his duties while piloting the bulk carrier Yangze 7 on July 19, 2024, when it collided with the towing vessel Miss Peggy near Lynchburg, Texas, according to the U.S. Department of Justice . The Miss Peggy capsized and sank with five crewmembers aboard. Four were rescued, while a fifth, identified in court records as 25-year-old deckhand Aquarius Lowman, was later found dead in the wreckage. One surviving crewmember suffered serious injuries and another sustained minor injuries. The indictment follows a National Transportation Safety Board investigation released in August that found the pilot had been distracted by an extended, nonoperational cellphone conversation with another pilot while navigating the busy waterway. Investigators determined that the call lasted 39 minutes and ended just two minutes and 16 seconds before the collision. The distraction contributed to the pilot’s failure to detect the Miss Peggy ahead of the bulk carrier. The NTSB also identified failures elsewhere on the vessels. The Yangze 7 bridge team did not detect the towboat until it was less than a ship’s length ahead, while the Miss Peggy captain failed to detect the bulk carrier approaching from astern. Investigators concluded that the collision resulted from a loss of situational awareness by the pilot, the bulk carrier’s bridge team and the towboat’s captain due to failures to maintain proper lookouts. The investigation also found that the Houston Pilots organization had no policy at the time prohibiting nonoperational use of personal electronic devices by pilots directing vessel movements. The NTSB subsequently recommended that the Coast Guard and American Pilots’ Association establish restrictions on such use. The American Pilots’ Association, responding to the NTSB findings in August, said the pilot’s performance had fallen short of professional standards and pledged to work with regulators to strengthen safeguards against distracted navigation. The collision caused an estimated $3.7 million in damages, salvage expenses and pollution mitigation costs, according to the NTSB. The criminal indictment now places the incident under a federal statute that allows prosecutors to pursue charges against maritime officers and others whose misconduct, negligence or inattention results in a death. If convicted, Jefferson faces up to 10 years in federal prison and a $250,000 fine. Jefferson is scheduled to make his initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Christina Bryan on November 24. The Coast Guard investigated the case, which is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Jason E. Corley. The allegations have not been proven in court, and Jefferson is presumed innocent unless convicted. ABC Affiliate WGNO via REUTERS The U.S. Coast Guard has established a temporary safety zone on the Mississippi River in New Orleans through December 11 as salvage crews prepare to recover the American Heritage river cruise ship, which capsized after being struck by a tanker last week. The temporary final rule, published Wednesday in the Federal Register, formalizes restrictions first imposed November 13 following the collision between the tanker Atlantic Asphalt and the docked American Cruise Lines vessel near the Crescent City Connection Bridge. The safety zone covers a one-mile stretch of the Lower Mississippi River between mile markers 95.5 and 96.5, extending 500 feet from the left descending bank, or east bank. Vessels and personnel are prohibited from entering the restricted area without authorization from the Captain of the Port of New Orleans. The Coast Guard said the restrictions are necessary because of potential debris in the water and hazards associated with salvage vessels, personnel and heavy equipment. Recovery operations are expected to take several weeks, although the safety zone may be canceled before December 11 if conditions permit. The zone does not amount to a monthlong shutdown of the Mississippi River. According to a November 16 update from the City of New Orleans, the alternate navigation channel remains closed, but limited two-way traffic is permitted through the main span of the Crescent City Connection Bridge. Deep-draft vessels and towing vessels pushing 10 or more barges remain restricted to one-way transit. The November 13 collision caused American Heritage to capsize alongside the pier, triggering a major rescue operation involving federal and local emergency responders and nearby commercial vessels. According to the National Transportation Safety Board, 190 passengers and crew were aboard the riverboat at the time of the accident, with 36 people hospitalized. All personnel aboard both vessels were accounted for. The NTSB is leading the investigation into the collision. A unified command comprising the Coast Guard and American Cruise Lines has been established to oversee lightering and salvage operations. Divers began inspecting the submerged vessel on November 15 to assess hull damage and help develop a recovery plan. Containment boom has also been deployed around the wreck as a precaution. New Orleans officials said Monday that an initial sheen had dissipated and no additional pollution had been observed. The Coast Guard said it will continue monitoring conditions and issue updated navigation restrictions as the salvage operation progresses. articles.summary: A potential strike at the nation’s busiest container port complex is back on the table after contract negotiations between waterfront employers and a union representing about 250 port security workers...

Join the leading maritime news network The shipping ports of Los Angeles (top left) and Long Beach are seen from the window of a commercial aircraft over Long Beach, California, U.S. March 13, 2023. REUTERS/Chris Helgren A potential strike at the nation’s busiest container port complex is back on the table after contract negotiations between waterfront employers and a union representing about 250 port security workers failed to produce a breakthrough. The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) warned Wednesday that members of International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 could walk off the job as early as 12:01 a.m. Saturday, November 21, when their latest contract extension expires. According to PMA, Tuesday’s negotiations ended with little progress, and the union has indicated it is unwilling to agree to another extension. The two sides are scheduled to meet again Friday, leaving little time to avert a potential disruption. Although Local 26 represents just 2% of the ILWU workforce at the ports, its members provide security at six container terminals responsible for more than half of the cargo moving through the Los Angeles-Long Beach port complex. Those terminals handle approximately 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo, according to PMA. The concern is that a strike by the watchmen could quickly spread beyond the 250 workers directly involved in the dispute. Thousands of longshore workers, marine clerks and foremen covered by separate labor agreements are expected to honor Local 26 picket lines, potentially bringing vessel operations, container movements and truck access to a halt at affected terminals. The dispute comes at a particularly sensitive time for the Southern California supply chain, with the ports handling heavy cargo volumes ahead of the holiday shopping season. A prolonged shutdown could disrupt rail and trucking operations, delay imports and exports, and create congestion extending well beyond the waterfront. Employers Detail Contract Offer PMA said its latest proposal includes a one-time $3,200 bonus for each Local 26 member and wage increases that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000. The association said the offer would also preserve fully employer-paid healthcare for active workers and retirees, which it values at more than $62,000 annually, while increasing annual pension benefits to as much as $93,200 for the longest-serving workers. PMA accused the union of making little movement on its demands despite more than a year of negotiations, including talks assisted by the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. The union’s response to the latest employer proposals was not immediately available. Local 26 members are responsible for checking identification and credentials at terminal gates, conducting security patrols and reporting safety concerns. Their previous labor agreement expired in July 2025, with workers continuing under a series of extensions. The dispute is separate from the coastwide labor agreement covering most West Coast dockworkers, which runs through 2028. Economic Stakes PMA pointed to an analysis by maritime economist John Martin estimating that the six affected terminals handled approximately 6.2 million containers in 2025 and supported nearly 4.2 million jobs nationwide through direct and indirect economic activity. The analysis attributed $885 billion in national economic activity to cargo moving through those facilities last year. That figure represents the economic activity associated with the terminals, not an estimate of losses from a potential strike. PMA warned that losses could mount rapidly if vessels are unable to discharge cargo and containers already inside the terminals cannot be moved out. articles.title: FMC Advisory — Documented Export Policies Must be Filed with the FMC by March 1 Each Year
articles.summary: In order to enable the timely and efficient movement of export cargo, ocean common carriers transporting containerized cargo are required to file documented export policies as set forth in 46 CFR 542.1(j), issued as part of the Commission’s final rule…
articles.body: FMC Advisory — Documented Export Policies Must be Filed with the FMC by March 1 Each Year Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 Image courtesy FMC In order to enable the timely and efficient movement of export cargo, ocean common carriers transporting containerized cargo are required to file documented export policies as set forth in 46 CFR 542.1(j), issued as part of the Commission’s final rule, “Definition of Unreasonable Refusal to Deal or Negotiate with Respect to Vessel Space Accommodations Provided by an Ocean Common Carrier” issued in 2024. Common carriers must annually submit their documented export policy on or before March 1 each year. 90 FR 30 (Jan. 2, 2025); see also 46 CFR 542.1(j)(1). Failure to file as set forth below will constitute a violation of a federal regulation. Filing Instructions Unless superseded by subsequent Commission order or filing instructions issued by the Commission: 1. Ocean common carriers must file their documented export policy with the Commission on or before March 1 each calendar year. A documented export policy should cover the period until the next policy is due for submission. Common carriers may file updated versions more frequently as needed. 2. Documents must be submitted in English, and any monetary terms shall be expressed in terms of U.S. currency. 3. Documented export policies must be submitted via email to: [email protected] . 4. Each of the following items must be addressed in a documented export policy. The Commission provides the following guidance on how a carrier can best address each topic: “Pricing strategies” – The common carrier’s criteria for pricing export cargo space in service contracts, tariffs, and spot rates, detailing key cost drivers and their relative importance, including operational costs, vessel capacity utilization, equipment inventory levels, equipment repositioning and trade imbalance, as well as a discussion of how these factors are incorporated into pricing; whether customers are notified within a pre-determined timeframe, and details as to what that timeframe is, before any changes to freight rates, surcharges, or fees are implemented. “Markets served” and “Services offered” – (1) Each geographic/export market in which the common carrier offers service, in reasonable detail. (2) The export services the common carrier makes available within each market, including routes, sailing frequency, service alternatives/substitutes, and conditions for negotiating and accepting export bookings, especially to the extent such conditions differ from conditions applied to import bookings. “Strategies for equipment provision” – How the common carrier determines the availability, allocation, and positioning of equipment in support of exports, including empty containers; how equipment inventory is monitored and allocated across the market served, including how inventory distribution affects equipment availability; how equipment shortages or other disruptions may affect bookings and mitigation strategies in place to anticipate and address such issues; how the common carrier’s policies and practices for determining and maintaining an adequate supply of containers/equipment based on cargo volume, type, and transport costs in the markets served. “Blank sailings” – The common carrier’s definition of blank sailings, policy and practices for cancelling sailings, including the timing and all communication mechanisms for notifying shippers of such blankings, and mitigation strategies to assist with export cargo bookings affected by blankings; how the cascading effects across schedules and operations are addressed. “Sweeper vessels” – A detailed explanation of the common carrier’s rules, practices, policies and/or performance targets concerning the designation, and the use, of sweeper vessels. Under the regulation, a sweeper vessel “means a vessel exclusively designated to load and move empty containers from a U.S. port for the purpose of transporting them to another designated location.” “Alternative remedies or assistance” – A detailed explanation of the common carrier’s rules, practices, policies and/or performance targets for providing alternative vessel space accommodations to an export shipper denied space, including the circumstances under which each alternative is considered or offered. A detailed explanation of how affected export shippers can request assistance and where such resources are found on the carrier’s website. 5. If any topics listed under 541.2(j)(1)(i), 541.2(j)(1)(ii), and/or 541.2(j)(1)(iii) are not addressed in a documented export policy because they are not applicable, the documented export policy should attest to this inapplicability clearly and unambiguously and provide a detailed factual explanation for non-applicability. 6. Submissions must be signed by a duly authorized officer of the regulated party with a copy of evidence of the officer’s authority. Each documented export policy must clearly identify the common carrier’s: FMC organization number, legal name, and all associated trade name(s) if applicable. This ensures that documented export policies are properly accredited to the correct organization and that a common carrier is not deemed to be in violation of the regulation. A documented export policy of a parent company may cover subsidiary companies in addition to the parent company. However, the documented export policy must clearly identify for the parent company and each subsidiary covered: the FMC organization number, the legal name of the company, and all associated trade name(s), if applicable. Unless such information is clearly identified, the FMC will consider the submission as applicable only to the parent company. Documented export policies will not be circulated outside of the Federal Maritime Commission. These documents, and the information contained therein, are not publicly disclosable, in whole or in part, including in response to requests under the Freedom of Information Act. Failure to file a documented export policy by March 1 constitutes a violation of a federal regulation. A person that violates a regulation or order of the Commission is liable to the United States Government for a civil penalty. 46 U.S.C. 41107(a). “Each day of a continuing violation is a separate violation,” with a current maximum penalty of $14,988 per violation, or $74,943 where the violation was willful and knowing. Id.; 46 CFR 506.4(d). Additionally, submission of knowingly fraudulent statements or misrepresentation in response to this requirement, or any other regulation or agency order, can result in criminal prosecution under 18 U.S.C. 1001, which, upon conviction, carries criminal penalties of a fine, up to five years of imprisonment, or both.

articles.body: Floating Production Outlook: Pipeline Looks Huge, But Not All Projects Are Created Equal Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Alisa Reiner , Contributor Alisa Reiner is an independent contributor. Alisa brings experience in both... November 18, 2026 Figure 1. World map of selected installed and future pipeline floating units. Map note: The map covers 327 geographically assigned FPSO and FLNG units across all recorded years. Five Available units have no first-production year or geographic deployment and are excluded. Only countries with recorded FPSO/FLNG projects are shaded; darker red indicates larger regional totals. GOM = Gulf of Mexico, LATAM = Latin America, APAC = Asia-Pacific. Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Figure 2. Regional floating infrastructure composition by type, all recorded years. Source: Floating Units Database, Intelatus Global Partners (October 2026); calculations by author. Figure 4. Planned and on-order floating units by expected first-production year, 2026–2035. Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Global floating hydrocarbons and electricity production and storage infrastructure (floating units) has a sizeable development pipeline through 2035, but the gap between identified projects and committed work is substantial. Intelatus Global Partners tracks 711 floating units worldwide, including 232 planned or on-order facilities with expected first-production dates in 2026–2035 . The commercial implications extend beyond floating unit construction. A deepwater FPSO in LATAM, a SEMI in the Gulf of Mexico, and an FSRU at a coastal terminal involve different mooring systems, installation sequences, and vessel requirements. For mooring suppliers and offshore support vessel owners, project maturity, water depth, and regional charter conditions will determine how much of the identified pipeline becomes executable work. A Large Fleet, but Not a Single Market Analysis covers 460 installed, 72 on order, 174 planned, and five available units. APAC leads the installed fleet with 137 units, followed by LATAM (93) and Africa (89). FPSOs account for 181 installed units, ahead of FSOs (74), FSRUs (48), and SEMIs (40) . APAC, LATAM, and Africa together account for 492 of the 711 recorded units, but their status mix distinguishes operating assets from prospective work (Figure 1). 174 planned units outnumber the 72 on order by more than two to one, and the main uncertainty is how much of that prospective work becomes contracted installations. Where the Units Are LATAM has 99 FPSOs among 145 units, whereas the Gulf of Mexico has 25 SEMIs and only ten FPSOs. The Mediterranean Sea is dominated by FSRUs (20 of 34 units), a different installation market from offshore production. \APAC has the largest regional fleet (217 units), spread across 74 FPSOs, 50 FSOs, 25 FSRUs, and other designs. Its 68 projects dated 2026–2035 span production, storage, and LNG import rather than one offshore installation profile. As for water depths, regional means are 1,564 m in LATAM, 1,402.3 m in the Gulf of Mexico, 889 m in Africa, 509 m in the Mediterranean Sea, 328 m in APAC, and 297 m in North Europe . However, APAC’s lower average masks considerable variation — Indonesia and India are emerging as markets for ultra-deepwater drilling. Yet a simple geographical unit count is an incomplete measure of supplier demand. Commercial interest is forward-looking. LATAM has 52 planned or on-order units dated 2026–2035, including 41 FPSOs; Brazil accounts for 30 projects and Guyana for 11. Its 21 units in 2031–2035 give it the largest regional pipeline for that later period. Africa has 41 planned or on-order units scheduled for 2026–2035, including 23 FPSOs and seven FLNG facilities. Nigeria accounts for 14 projects, while Namibia has six. All 13 African units dated 2031–2035 remain planned, so their conversion into installation work still depends on project sanction and procurement. The Gulf of Mexico features 21 planned or on-order units dated 2026–2035, including nine SEMIs, versus four FPSOs and four FLNG facilities. Its prospective installation mix therefore differs materially from FPSO-led LATAM. FPSOs Drive the Production Pipeline Of the 232 planned or on-order facilities dated 2026–2035, 108 are FPSOs (47%), compared with 30 FLNG units, 33 FSRUs, 15 SEMIs, and 17 FSOs (Table 1). The remaining 29 units are other floating infrastructure types. Notably, interest in FLNG is broadening. Yinson Production , an established FPSO operator, is looking to extend its lease-and-operate model to FLNG, applying its experience in development, construction, and operations to offshore gas projects. In Brazil, Petrobras has sought market information on potential FLNG options for its offshore gas resources. Rystad Energy expects global FLNG capacity to rise from 14.1 Mtpa in 2024 to 42 Mtpa by 2030 and 55 Mtpa by 2035, supported by stronger operating performance and the economics of smaller or remote gas fields. The IEA projects more than 330 bcm/year of new LNG export capacity entering service over 2025–2030. This includes onshore plants as well as floating facilities, but the sheer scope is illustrative. T he Schedule Gets Less Certain After 2030 Expected first production peaks in 2028 at 52 units, evenly split between 26 on order and 26 planned (Figure 3). This is not the offshore installation peak: mooring pre-lay and floater hook-up normally occur before first production, and project delays could shift that workload across years. Project maturity is a greater uncertainty than the precise annual profile. Of the 164 units dated 2026–2030, 70 are on order and 94 are planned. In 2031–2035, just two are on order and 66 remain planned. Schedules can move, and some developments may never reach sanction. Conversely, newly added projects could increase demand after 2030. Importantly, the installed fleet is not a static base to which all pipeline projects can simply be added. Some units will retire; others will remain on their fields longer, be modified, or be redeployed. The database does not contain a complete schedule of retirements and redeployments, so the identified pipeline is not a forecast of net fleet growth. Similarly, redeployment does not necessarily require building a new hull, but it could involve repair, new moorings, underwater operations, and reinstatement. Mooring Design Determines Installation Scope Floater architecture and field conditions determine the mooring scope. A turret-moored FPSO, spread-moored SEMI, and tension-leg platform transmit station-keeping loads differently and require different installation sequences. Water depth, metocean loading, and seabed conditions affect mooring geometry, line length, strength, materials, and anchor choice, including whether drag-embedment, suction, or torpedo anchors are suitable. These choices set vessel and handling requirements. A typical deepwater chain–polyester–chain system can involve separate campaigns for anchor installation, line pre-lay, and floater hook-up. Installation loads and methods, rather than floater type alone, determine anchor handling tug supply (AHTS) vessels’ bollard pull, winch and deck capacity, and the number of loadouts required. A single development can therefore generate work across floating facilities, moorings, and subsea systems. For suppliers, this makes a combined assessment of floater type and regional conditions essential — it is their interaction that determines the technical specifications of mooring systems, installation requirements, and ultimately the type and capacity of offshore support vessels (OSV) needed. Charter Markets Shape OSV Availability Market factors also matter. Charter terms can restrict the pool of suitable vessels for other projects. For instance, in Brazil, DOF secured four-year awards for four AHTS vessels, including one with more than 350 tons of bollard pull and three configured for deepwater remotely operated vehicle (ROV) vessel work. Such long-term commitments secure utilization for owners while limiting high-specification vessel availability elsewhere. North Sea vessel tightness in 2025-2026 has been partly linked to longer Brazilian commitments. Conversely, West Africa is more short-term campaign-driven: vessels often get mobilized there from the North Sea, moving south during the northern hemisphere winter. Summer returns are possible, not automatic; mobilization costs, contract terms, local requirements, and weather windows govern the economics. The Commercial Outlook The key message is that the floating market should be read as a portfolio of very different offshore campaigns rather than a single global trend. LATAM remains the deepest pool of FPSO demand, but it is also one of the markets where large, long-duration projects can tie up high-specification tonnage and absorb substantial mooring scope. APAC is broader and less uniform: it combines production, storage, and gas infrastructure, while parts of the region are now moving further into deepwater. Africa offers both established FPSO work and a growing gas-related story, but much of the later pipeline still has to convert from planning into funded execution. For suppliers, that means market entry should be based on technical fit and regional positioning, not just on the headline number of units. The more forward-looking point is that project quality now matters more than project count. The 2026–2030 pipeline contains the bulk of identified near-term work, but after 2030 the market becomes more gas-heavy and much less certain, with most units still only planned. That creates a premium for companies that can screen pipelines early, follow the shift from concept to commitment, and match vessels, moorings, and installation methods to the projects most likely to move. In practice, the winners are likely to be those positioned where three conditions overlap: a credible project backlog, technical complexity that limits competition, and local market access. That is where floating-unit activity turns into real commercial demand.
